# PREFACE.

The almost universal and highly commendable interest, which many ecclesiastical and secular persons of rank <note>The author refers to both church leaders and government officials, highlighting that support for the Waldensians was both a religious and a political matter in the Dutch Republic.</note> in the Netherlands, driven by a new zeal, currently take in the welfare of the renowned church communities, which are located in the low valleys of remote *Piedmont*; <note>Piedmont is a region in northwest Italy. The Waldensians lived in specific "Valleys" there, often facing isolation and persecution.</note> --- this interest, which indeed adds such excellent luster to our Fatherland, and now provides abundant evidence that its yearning for the welfare of CHRIST'S CHURCH in other parts of the world is not extinguished, nor has the old, highly praised Charity <term>Mildadigheid: A specific Dutch cultural concept of religious-based philanthropy and international aid, for which the Dutch Republic was famous in the 18th century.</term> for the support and refreshment of infirm and impoverished fellow believers died out; --- this interest, and this reason, I say, has among many other reasons, which I have judged appropriate to mention more broadly in the following first chapter, encouraged me, in hours of leisure, to gain for myself, through further investigation of the state of the Waldensians, <note>The Waldensians (Waldenzen) were a proto-Protestant group that survived for centuries in the Alps despite numerous attempts by the Dukes of Savoy and the Catholic Church to suppress them.</note> a more accurate knowledge of their—

# PREFACE.

...to provide for their earlier and later Fates <note>The author uses "Lotgevallen" to describe the series of events, both fortunate and tragic, that defined the Waldensian experience.</note>, and afterwards to share what I had discovered about them with my fellow countrymen.

The Reader will perhaps wonder to see a great work of wide scope handled in a small little book; and ask why a COMPLETE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY <term>Ecclesiastical History: A genre of writing, popular in the 18th century, that chronicled the development, struggles, and survival of Christian denominations.</term> of that people, who have sent such a name for themselves out into the world; who have undergone so many political upheavals; so often prosperity and adversity; sometimes a pleasant peace, and at other times such horrific destructions, for nearly XVIII <note>18</note> Centuries, is presented in such a concise summary?

In my own defense, I will gladly admit that it would indeed have cost me much time, but no heavy labor, to describe in more than one large volume the Histories of the Waldensians <note>The Waldenzen (Waldensians) were a medieval movement that the author, following the traditions of his time, believes can be traced back to the early Christian era.</note>, from the times of the Apostles, or their immediate successors, up until the present day, and particularly

# P R E F A C E .

to show the recent Fates <note>The Dutch "Lotgevallen" refers to the series of events, both fortunate and tragic, that happen to someone over time.</note> at great length; but who takes pleasure in reading previously printed Writings, published anew? Who is pleased to find things, which are more or less known, repeated all over again? Or who desires to see matters, which can be settled in a short space—without that brevity giving birth to obscurity or significant matters being overlooked—presented in a long and tedious manner, to the loss of one's desire to read?

To avoid this writing style, which is unpleasant to me and, as I trust, also to my Readers, I have endeavored, as much as possible, to keep alive and earn the interest and attention of my Readers through this brevity of mine; being of the opinion that, since I have skipped no event of importance as far as I am aware, this concise narrative would be sufficient to give the charitable Netherlands <note>The "charitable Netherlands" refers to the Dutch Republic’s historical role as a sanctuary and financial supporter for persecuted Protestant groups across Europe.</note> an idea of the formerly famous, now less known, very impoverished Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement that sought to return to apostolic poverty and simplicity; they faced centuries of persecution by the authorities.</note>, and

## CHAPTER I.
### Introduction.

If it is judged useful to preserve the histories of the Kingdoms and Commonwealths <term>Commonwealths: Referring to the Dutch 'Gemeenebesten,' or republics, specifically the United Provinces of the Netherlands</term> of this world from oblivion, then everyone who has any regard for the true religion must readily agree that it is a significant undertaking to record the fates of Christ’s church in general, and of its congregations in particular. This is especially true of those congregations which, amidst a constant alternation of oppression and prosperity, have remained steadfast in the sincere confession of the faith of the Saints once delivered <note>A biblical allusion to Jude 1:3, "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints," emphasizing the perceived antiquity and purity of Waldensian belief</note>. Nowhere does Divine Providence shine more brightly than in the faithful preservation and repeated deliverance of those who call upon His name. Nothing is more capable of making such believers—who enjoy freedom of conscience under a merciful government of their fellow-believers, as the **Dutch** can pride themselves on—truly realize the greatness of their invaluable privileges. It serves to awaken a recognition of God’s mercies and to encourage the imitation of the illustrious examples of those sincere people, should a cloud of persecution unexpectedly disturb the land and the church.

## CHAPTER I.
### Introduction.

If it is considered useful to preserve the histories of the kingdoms and republics <term>Republics: The original Dutch term "Gemeene-besten" refers to common-wealths or republics, specifically alluding to the Dutch Republic</term> of this world from oblivion, then everyone who has any regard for true religion must readily agree that it is a significant undertaking to record the fortunes of Christ’s church in general, and of its congregations <term>Congregations: In this context, the Dutch "Gemeintens" refers to specific local bodies of believers or faith communities</term> in particular. 

This is especially true of those congregations which, amidst a constant alternation of oppression and prosperity, have remained steadfast in the sincere confession of the faith once delivered to the saints. Nowhere does Divine Providence shine more clearly than in the faithful preservation and repeated deliverance of those who call upon His name. Nothing is better suited to make such believers—who enjoy freedom of conscience <note>The right to follow one's religious convictions without state interference</note> under a benevolent government of their fellow believers, as the Dutch can boast of here—rightly realize the greatness of their invaluable privileges. It serves to awaken them to a recognition of God’s mercies or to the imitation of the illustrious examples of those sincere people, should a cloud of persecution unexpectedly trouble their land and church.

<header>ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY</header>

The consideration of these things justifies my effort to preserve from oblivion the final fortunes of a small, poor, and humble, yet no less God-fearing people. In ancient times, they were the glory of the Christian church—or let me rather say that in the most ignorant times <note>Refers to the Middle Ages, often called the "Dark Ages" by later Protestant historians</note>, they were the only light of the world. By doing so, I offer my fellow countrymen new material for pious reflection and labor primarily for the glorification of the great Savior through a tale of great and wonderful events.

For what people, indeed, what church congregation is like that of the *Waldensians* <term>Waldensians: A medieval movement (dating back to the 12th century) that emphasized apostolic poverty and the Bible as the sole authority, frequently persecuted by the Roman Catholic Church</term>? Since the times of the *Apostles*, they have remained standing unchanged until this day in the public, pure confession and zealous practice of the Christian religion, despite all enemies. Which church, like this one, has never fallen into any heresy? Which congregation has striven so courageously against idolatry and superstition? Could *Calvin* and *Luther* <note>Leaders of the 16th-century Protestant Reformation</note> ever contest their precedence in this? Which land is more flooded with red pools of blood, shed by dying saints? Where has one ever found a handful of people who, for two hundred years, waged the heaviest wars without flinching against the mightiest worldly princes? In a word, where has Divine power and goodness in the preservation and rescue of a lowly people from the mouth of the lions ever shone more visibly than among the *Waldensians*? 

And must it not most of all strike our attention that in their land—though bordering *Italy*, the seat of Roman power and glory, and also the place where the greatest vices and taints have reigned and are not yet entirely rooted out—they have nevertheless kept their clothes unstained <note>A biblical reference to Revelation 3:4, implying spiritual purity amidst corruption</note>? Indeed, they have remained so under the sovereignty of Roman princes...

many centuries until this day, through a miraculous Providence <note>The theological concept that God intervenes in the world to protect the faithful</note>, have remained standing. Does the memory of this renowned people not then deserve to be preserved until the end of all ages? And how will the truth of our Religion not be given the strongest support through a discourse on such remarkable events? Will the objections of the Roman Catholics—that our Reformed Church first raised its head in the time of *Luther* and *Calvin*—not appear childish, when we can demonstrate from manifold proofs, and even from their own writings, that the *Waldensians* have adhered to the Doctrine of truth from the times of the Apostles until now? Will unbelief and godlessness, now emerging more than ever from the hellish abyss <note>A likely reference to Enlightenment-era skepticism or atheism</note>, appear attractive to unpracticed minds, when we can confirm the certainty of the Gospel and the firmness of the Divine promises from the fates of the *Waldensians*? Weighty reasons, in my judgment, which give me full leave to preserve the events of this ancient and renowned people from oblivion.

The name *Waldensians* has now become a very unfamiliar word to many: one hardly knows if that church still exists, and very few know their most recent events and current condition.

In the previous century <note>The 17th century, a period of significant Dutch support for persecuted Protestants abroad</note>, several histories of that renowned people were published; the general interest that the *Netherlands* took in their preservation at that time made the publication of those writings necessary, for various reasons. But one must excuse me—as I am no lover of merely copying out histories already printed in our language, which anyone can look up—for quoting little or nothing from them. I

# CHURCH HISTORY

I shall content myself with naming the principal writers, from whom the inquisitive reader—should they be unsatisfied with the Short Sketch I intend to give of the earliest histories of the *Waldensians*—might further satisfy their interest.

The first to be considered here is the *History of the Reformed Churches in the Valleys of Piedmont, called Waldensians, described in French by P. Gillis and translated by G. van Breen, Minister in Beverwijk, printed at Amsterdam 1663.* — as well as *B. Lydius, Three Historical Treatises, Dordrecht 1624.* — as also *Perrin, History of the Albigenses and Waldensians.* <note>The Albigenses were a medieval religious group in Southern France, often associated by Protestant historians with the Waldensians as "pre-Reformation" heroes.</note> — *D. S. Korte, Chronicle of the Waldensians, Amsterdam 1657.* — *History of the Waldensians, Amsterdam 1732. first Volume (*).* One may add here the Martyr Books of *Mellinus* and *van Bracht.* <note>These refer to Abraham Mellinus's *History of the Martyrs* and Thieleman J. van Braght's *Martyrs Mirror*, the latter being a cornerstone of Mennonite history.</note> In French, one may consult the beautiful work of *J. Leger, History of the Vaudois <note>original: "Histoire des Vaudois"</note>, Leiden 1699. 2 vols. in folio.* — *P. Boyer, Abridgement of the History of the Vaudois <note>original: "Abregé de l'Histoire des Vaudois"</note>, 1691. first part, the sequel being, as far as I know, never printed.* — Further, *Basnage, History of the Religion of the Reformed Churches <note>original: "Histoire de la Religion des Eglises Reformées"</note>, Rotterdam 1725.* — *The Magdeburg Centuries <note>original: "Centur. Magdeburgens." — A massive 16th-century Protestant work on church history organized by centuries.</note>, Century XII.* — *Pictet, History of the 11th & 12th Century <note>original: "Histoire du XI. & XII. Siecle"</note> Amsterdam.*

(*) This last fine little work, containing the fates of the Waldensians in the first twelve centuries, was published without the name of the learned author: I have been informed, and am fully assured, that we have the Reverend Mr. *M. Schagen* to thank for it. He is a Mennonite <note>original: "Doopsgezinde"</note> Minister in Utrecht, who is well known in our Fatherland for his pious writings and the successful translations of *Bennet’s* "Religious Christian," *Hervey’s* "Theron and Aspasio," and *Pearsall’s* "Contemplations." <note>Marten Schagen (1700–1770) was a prominent book collector and scholar. The English works he translated were popular devotional texts of the time.</note> Lack of time, so that industrious Teacher writes to me, has prevented me from fulfilling my objective with that History, and it is not to be expected that I shall have enough leisure hours remaining to work further on it (namely, on the second and third volumes).

*Amsterdam 1732.* — *Bossuet, Universal History <note>original: "Histoire Universelle"</note>, vol. 3.* — *du Pin, Library of Ecclesiastical Authors <note>original: "Bibliotheque des Auteurs Eccles."</note> Vol. XXII.* — *Sermon on Matthew 10:42* by *G. Wake*, Archbishop of Canterbury 1699. — and the recently printed French and German *Sermon on Galatians 6:10* by the prematurely deceased Middelburg minister *de Loo*.

However, some of these authors end their history very early: *Gillis* goes no further than the year 1656. *Boyer* extends his brief account only to 1690. *Basnage* follows him in this, yet both are very brief in reporting the events of the two very famous years of 1686 and 1689.

I will not hide that, in order to give the reader a true account of two of the most remarkable events that ever occurred in the Valleys—I mean the wretched expulsion of the *Waldensians* from their fatherland in the year 1686, and their return to the same in the year 1689, of which nothing has ever been read in our language <note>The author refers to the Dutch language.</note>—I have made use of two pieces written in French, which are currently less known to my countrymen. # ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

I will content myself with naming the principal writers, from whom the inquisitive reader—should they not be satisfied with the *Brief Sketch* which I intend to give of the earliest histories of the *Waldensians*—might further satisfy their desire.

The first to be considered here is the *History of the Reformed Churches in the Valleys of Piedmont, called Waldensians* <note>original: "Historie van de Gereformeerde Kerken in de Valleyen van Piemont, genaamd Waldenzen"</note>, described in French by *P. ## CHAPTER II.

->*On the name of the Waldensians and their Valleys,*<-
->*alongside their Form of Government.*<-

Regarding the name of the Waldensians, there is no people who, in ancient times, were named in so many different ways (*) and became known to the world in such a manner. Sometimes they were given a name after their most famous Teachers (†); at other times after the Doctrine they so zealously professed (§); then after the Country they inhabited (‡); and not infrequently, in order to revile them, they were distinguished from other nations by all sorts of mocking and abusive names.

---

(*) Hottinger, *Ecclesiastical History, 12th Century*, p. 281.
(†) Henricians, Josephines, Arnoldists, Lollards, etc. <note>These were various medieval reform movements often grouped together by the established church.</note> G. Brandt, *History of the Reformation*, p. 26.
(§) Fratricelli <note>original: "Little Brothers"</note>, Insabbatati <note>original: "Insabbatarii"; likely referring to their footwear or their refusal to observe certain feast days</note>, Apostolics, etc. *The Dutch Sulpitius* by J. Baselius, p. 182.
(‡) Turlupins, Transmontanes <note>original: "Transmontani", meaning "those from across the mountains"</note>, Chienards <note>A derogatory term likely derived from the French word for "dog"</note>, etc. Lampe, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, Chapter 9, Section 27.

### OF THE WALDENSIANS.
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

the (*); but the most commonly used and best-known name for this People in the previous and current Century has been that of *Vaudois* or *Waldensians*.

Several men of standing have greatly erred regarding the origin and derivation of this last-mentioned word. Some derive the word *Waldensians* from the word *Walden*, keeping in view the *Woods* and *Forests* <note>The Dutch word 'wouden' and German 'Walden' refer to forests, suggesting the name means 'forest-dwellers.'</note> of the *Alpine* mountains they inhabited; others from the French word *Vallées*, meaning *Valleys*; not a few believe that they received the name from *Peter Waldo*, a famous merchant in *Lyons* in *France* (†). However, it appears from an ancient manuscript (§), donated by the learned *Morland* <note>Sir Samuel Morland (1625–1695) was an English diplomat who served as Oliver Cromwell's envoy to the Duchy of Savoy to protest the persecution of the Waldensians.</note>, Envoy of *England*, to the Library of *Cambridge* and preserved there, that they already bore the name of *Waldensians* 70 years before the time of *Peter Waldo*. Much rather, one rightly thinks that *Peter Waldo*—whose actual name is not exactly known due to various reports (‡)—derived his name from the *Waldensians* (**). The most likely and certain conclusion is that the name *Waldensians* originates from the Land inhabited by them. In their language, which is a mixture of *Italian* and *French*, the words—

---

(*) *Gazari, Piphles, Passagians, Circumcised, Gynici, Publicans, Cabatati* etc. <note>These were all derogatory terms or labels for heretical groups used by medieval authorities.</note> Lampe, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, ch. 10, § 54.
(†) *Hottinger, Ecclesiastical History, 12th Century, p. 278.*
(§) *J. Leger*, in his *History of the Vaudois*, gives us a brief extract of this precious piece, in which one finds these words regarding the name of the *Waldensians*:
> "They say that he is a Vaudois, and is worthy of death." <note>original: "Illi dison quel es Vaudé, s e degne de murir." This is in Old Occitan, the native language of the Waldensian valleys.</note>
(‡) *Petrus Baldo*, or *Baldon* as called by some; by others *Valdo* or *Valdoni, Valdio, Valdus* and *Waldus*.
(**) *J. van den Honert, Oration on the Bohemian and Moravian Church* p. 12. *Lampe, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, Ch. 10, § 5.* and others.

the Valleys are called *Valli* or *Vaux*, and they themselves *Valdesi*, that is, Inhabitants of the Dales or Valleys (*): from this, Latin writers call them *Valdenses*, from which the word *Waldensians* could very easily have arisen.

These *Waldensians* have lived since time immemorial in the *Valleys of Piedmont*, which is a part of old *Lombardy*, situated in *Upper Italy* (†), bordering to the North on *Savoy*, to the West on *France*, to the *South* on the *Mediterranean Sea* and the territory of the Republic of *Genoa*, and to the East on the Duchies of *Montferrat* and *Milan*. From the South to the North, *Piedmont* is thirty geographical miles in size, but from the West to the East much less (§). This Duchy, whose capital is *Turin*, bears the name of *Piedmont*, because it is located at the foot of the *Alps*, a great mountain range that separates *France* from *Savoy* (‡). These *Alps* consist of a great multitude of sky-high mountains and rocks, at the foot of which one finds many valleys and nearly inaccessible dales, miraculously protected by the Almighty Creator, and therefore inhabited by those who [fled] the heavy persecutions of their enemies

->## OF THE WALDENSIANS.<-

fleeing the [persecutions], have from time to time settled in these Dales and remained there. If one did not note this on this occasion, it would seem incredible—as will be heard several times in the following pages—how a handful of people were able to defend themselves against the heaviest attacks of the mightiest armies and repel them.

*Piedmont* itself is divided into the Province of *Turin*, the *Canavese District*, the *Marquisate of Susa*, the *Lucerna Territory*—otherwise called the *Valleys of Piedmont*, or sometimes simply called the *Valleys* (*)—and furthermore into several other provinces, which are unnecessary to list here.

The *Valleys* inhabited by the *Waldensians* are three in number.

I. The first is that of *Lucerna* (†), 15 *Piedmontese miles* long; yet very unequal in width, being separated to the West from the *Valley of Queyras* by the so-called *Cross Hill* <note>original: "kruisheuvel"; likely referring to the Col de la Croix, a mountain pass between France and Italy.</note>, where the *River Pellice*, which waters nearly the entire Valley, originates. In this Valley are seven congregations of the *Waldensians*, namely *Bobbio*, *Villars*, *Torre Pellice*, *Rora*, *San Giovanni*, *Angrogna*, and *Rocheplatte*.

---

(*) One must not confuse the *Valleys of Piedmont* with other *Dales*. The Valleys found in the *Cottian Alps*, in the *Marquisates of Saluzzo and Susa*, were all formerly inhabited by *Waldensians*. Many were also found towards the side of *Dauphiné* as far as *Embrun* and *Briançon*, but as their numbers grew, they spread into *Provence* and *Languedoc*, where they were called *Albigensians* <note>The Albigensians (or Cathars) were a medieval religious group in Southern France who, like the Waldensians, were targeted by the Catholic Church, most notably during the Albigensian Crusade.</note>, who today are entirely exterminated. *Piedmont's Valleys* are only three in number.

(†) From ancient times, this Valley has carried a burning *torch surrounded by darkness* in its *coat of arms*, from which the name of *Lucerna* <note>From the Latin *lucerna*, meaning "lamp" or "lantern."</note> presumably originated. No coat of arms suited it better, as the joyful *light of the Gospel* has always shone in the same, even in the darkest times.

<center>A</center>

The congregation of *Bobbio* is situated the highest; it produces chestnuts, wine, and grain, and is surrounded by high *Alps* bearing various names.

In the congregation of *Villars*, one finds little flat land, yet what is there is exceptionally fertile: to the south one finds chestnuts and good pastureland; on the hills to the north, wine and grain.

*Torre Pellice* <note>original: "La Tour"</note> takes its name from an ancient high tower, in whose place the Duke of *Savoy* had a fortress built in 1655 for the suppression of the *Waldensians*.

The congregation of *San Giovanni* <note>Saint John</note> has, in part, a pleasant plain with the most beautiful meadows along the *Pellice* River; in part, a field where grapevines and tilled land are found together. Here, the farmer grows the finest grain under trees and vineyards that are spread on laths from one trunk to another—vines under which the *Waldensians* often hid themselves during times of persecution. Besides the beautiful fruit trees, one finds here a multitude of mulberry trees, which the inhabitants use to the benefit of their silkworms.

The region of the congregation of *Angrogna*, watered by a small stream of the same name, is generally mountainous and yields almost no wine, but many chestnuts and other good fruits, and especially an abundance of good pasture for the cattle. It is by nature uncommonly strong <note>In a military or defensive sense.</note>, as it can only be approached from below on two sides—namely from the south and the east. Even if it were to be taken through treachery or force, the inhabitants have an almost inaccessible and well-secured refuge on Mount *Vachera* or in the so-called Tower Meadow (*): these

### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

last place consists of a great hollow between the highest mountains, which one can reach only with the greatest difficulty. This spacious cavern can contain a multitude of people, and the *Waldensians* used it in times of heavy persecution to hide their teachers and to allow their young *Nazirites* <note>In this context, "Nazirites" refers to the young men studying to become "Barbes" or pastors, who often lived ascetic lives dedicated to their studies.</note> to continue their studies in peace.

II. The second Valley is that of *Perosa*, a journey of four hours long, though of uneven width, the widest part being one hour across. It takes its name from a town, or rather a small fortress, which lies on its heights and protects the approaches of the Rivers *Chisone* and *Germanasca*, as well as those of the Valleys of *St. Martin* and *Chisone*. It has little flat land, and what there is is intersected by the River *Chisone*, into which the *Germanasca* flows. On the southern side, fruits of all kinds grow in abundance, but no wine; however, wine is found plentifully to the north, where the city of *Pinerolo* is situated. In this Valley, one counts three congregations of the *Waldensians*, namely those of *St. Germain*, *Pramol*, and *Pomaret*.

III. The third Valley bears the name of *St. Martin*, so called after a nearly desolate place where the ruins of a church dedicated to that saint are still found. This Valley is 16 *Piedmontese* miles long, but not much wider than the River *Germanasca* flowing through it. Toward the bottom one finds many grapevines and other fruits, in the middle chestnuts, and at the top beautiful meadows. This Valley is by nature the best protected and fortified. The three Valleys are generally quite pleasant due to their fertility, yet one should not think that everything grows there without effort and danger, for the melting snow, falling down in great clumps from the highest Mountain peaks, sometimes carries stones of a violent size down with it, threatening the Farmer with certain death, or at least ruining his sown field, and shattering his tender grapevine. Also the fertility decreases as one comes higher up; the hills, however, are only [suitable] for Chestnuts and

->### OF THE WALDENSIANS.<-

[capable of bearing] other fruits: on the medium-height mountains one finds forests of tall trees, interspersed with hedges and shrubs, and the peaks of the highest mountains are mostly covered with thick snow and heavy ice floes.

A particular language is spoken in these Valleys, being a mixture of Italian and French with one another <note>This likely refers to Occitan or the Piedmontese dialect, which share features with both major languages</note>. The inhabitants are clever and would, if they had all the necessary freedom and opportunity to train themselves well, go far in the sciences. The Land is Roman <note>meaning Roman Catholic</note>. The Pope has little authority in ecclesiastical matters, but the Duke, who is currently also King of Sardinia, has much.

In the beginning of the 13th Century, the Valleys, previously always governed by their own Princes, were brought under the Dominion of the House of **Savoy** (*). ***Thomas***, Duke of ***Savoy***, made himself master of the City of ***Pignerol*** <note>Modern-day Pinerolo</note> and the Valleys in the year 1233, under the pretext that the ancestral house of the Princes of ***Piedmont*** had become extinct (†). The Waldensians submitted to this new ruler on the condition that they would be preserved in their old privileges, which he granted them and which was confirmed by his successors. The current Royal House of **Savoy** long assumed the title of "Royal Highness" by virtue of a claim to the ancient Kingdom of **Cyprus**, yet held no more than the dignity of Dukes of **Savoy** and **Piedmont** until the year 1713, when ***Victor Amadeus II***, in a Peace treaty with ***France*** <note>The Treaty of Utrecht</note>, obtained the Kingdom of **Sicily**, and thereafter had himself crowned King in Palermo. The 12th Century is remarkable for the decrees of several Popes who, being unable to tolerate the *Waldensians’* great knowledge of the Holy Scriptures nor their godliness of life, which shone like a light in the darkness, began to concern themselves with them more than ever.

Pope *Alexander* III opened the scene with his ban <note>a formal ecclesiastical prohibition or excommunication</note>, yet with little fruit, for they increased so greatly in number that the Valleys could no longer contain so many inhabitants. Some, then, lured by the charming countryside of fertile *Italy*, went to seek a residence in *Calabria* and *Apulia*.

Those who remained in the Valleys applied themselves more zealously than ever during this time to the sciences, particularly to Theology <term>Godgeleerdheid: the formal study of religious truth and the nature of God</term>, in which they made great progress. They even gave lessons in Medicine, Mechanics <note>referring to the physical sciences or engineering of the time</note>, and other fine sciences to their youths. Some Teachers undertook great journeys and maintained communications with their fellow believers in *England*, *Germany*, *Gascony*, *Provence*, *Dauphiné*, and *Calabria*.

Pope *Lucius* III, noticing this progress, made new decrees against them (†), and Pope *Innocentius* III, successor of *Cælestinus* III, stirred up the Inquisition <note>the judicial institution of the Roman Catholic Church established to find and suppress heresy</note> against them in the year 1198, which plan was likewise followed by *Honorius* III; yet these thunderbolts of excommunication from the Roman Vatican did little harm to the Valleys.

## CHAPTER V.

### *A brief Sketch of the Events in the Valleys, from the XII Century to the year 1655.*

**T**he XIII Century provides us with several testimonies of the propagation of their Doctrine and their steadfastness in its Profession. A certain Roman Catholic writer of that time complains about this, stating that the poison of unbelief spread ever further (*): another writer, *Matthew Paris* <note>a Benedictine monk and English chronicler known for his history of the world</note>, in his narrative of the year 1234, having charged them with many false accusations, must finally confess to their honor that they steadfastly continued to oppose Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiatie: the Roman Catholic dogma that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual substance of the body and blood of Christ</term>. Until now, one had never heard of Jesuits <note>members of the Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order</note>, Missionaries, or Inquisitors in the Valleys, which had indeed contributed much to the prosperity of the *Waldensians*; and some of the Priests who were in the Valleys, being convinced that the true Doctrine was found here, kept quiet and did not wish to oppose them, while others remained silent for different reasons.

In this Century, the Valleys came under a different administration: until now, they had been governed by their own Princes; but in the year 1233, *Thomas*, son of *Humbert*, Duke of *Savoy*, took *Pignerol* <note>modern-day Pinerolo</note>, the capital of the Valleys of *Piedmont*, along with several other places, claiming that, because the dynasty of *Piedmont’s* Princes had become extinct, he [should take] the control of these

After they had issued heavy Bulls <term>Bull: a formal decree issued by a Pope</term> against the *Waldensians*, they had the most prominent among them put to death, hoping that the others would thereby renounce the so-called Heresy. The same Archbishop, seeing no desired result from this, proceeded to gather 99 reports to understand the true state of the Valleys; from these, it became clear to him that almost all inhabitants of the Valleys were infected with the so-called Heresy. He then decided in the year 1486 to command them to depart from the Valleys; but not heeding his orders, they flatly refused this. This embittered him and the Pope immensely: neither soft nor hard remedies could turn the increasing *Waldensians* away from their Doctrine, and everything seemed to have been attempted in vain, except for the most severe measures, which, to avoid the extreme, had not yet been tried. Pope *Innocent VIII* decided to employ the extreme for their eradication, and thereupon, in the following year 1487, sent his Legate, *Albertus de Capitaneis* <note>also known as Albert Cataneo</note>, to the Courts of various Kings and Princes, with the request to eradicate this destructive Heresy with united forces all at once. *Leger* <note>Jean Léger (1615–1670), a Waldensian pastor and historian</note> says (*): that on that occasion, more than eight hundred thousand Reformers <note>original: *Hervormden*; Léger uses this term retrospectively for the Waldensians and other early dissenting groups</note> were killed in *Europe*. They called this war, which was also waged against the *Waldensians* in *Piedmont*, a holy war; and *Innocent* promised indulgence <term>Indulgence: a remission of the temporal punishment for sin, often granted by the Church in exchange for service or piety</term> of sins and the possession of the goods and lands of those who were about to be killed to those who signed up for this war (†). In *Dauphiné*, *Languedoc*, and *Provence*, much blood was shed on this occasion, yet the Pope had taken special, cruel care for the *Piedmontese* Valleys, being unable to tolerate that the Heresy flourished most gloriously in a place so near to *Italy*. An army of 18,000 men, besides a great multitude of volunteers, attacked the Valleys. The *Waldensians*, having lived in peace for so many centuries (except for having suffered an occasional specific persecution by the *Inquisition*) and consequently being unaccustomed to war, stood this violent shock bravely. God was for

[God was with] them, and who, being against them, could then stand? The enemy's army was repulsed, driven away, and heavily damaged by their brave resistance, so that its remains had to stay at the borders of the Valleys and could achieve nothing further than merely raiding the flat countryside. *Philip* VII, Duke of *Savoy* and Prince of *Piedmont*, not finding his account <note>meaning he found the war neither profitable nor successful</note> in this war, nor gaining any honor through desired victories, and seeing that his Roman <note>original: *Roomsche*; referring to Roman Catholic</note> subjects had suffered greatly from the war at the same time, decided no longer to let himself be incited by the Pope, but to make peace with the *Waldensians*. He generously confessed that the bad impressions of them that had been instilled in him were the cause of the persecution: he now called them his loyal subjects and promised to preserve them in all their liberties from then on.

This outcome of affairs breathed new courage into the *Waldensians*. The peace gave them the opportunity to further propagate their doctrine, so that at the beginning of the XV century <note>The text says "XV" (15th), though the context suggests the author is discussing the late 15th leading into the 16th century</note>, Roman priests in the prominent city of *Florence* were heard complaining to the people in their public sermons from their pulpits that *Florence* should no longer be called the flower of *Italy*, since the *Waldensians* had persuaded it that man was justified not by works, but by faith.

In this century, the news of the Reformation begun in *Switzerland* and *Germany* reached the Valleys, and was received with so much joy that in the year 1526, several prominent men were sent out to those regions to learn what the truth of this matter was. The envoys held a conversation with *Bucer* <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a German Protestant reformer based in Strasbourg</note>, *Zwingli* <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), the leader of the Reformation in Switzerland</note> and

# ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

the year 1560. nothing more can be said than that the renowned Historian *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a prominent French historian and statesman; his works are often cited for their relative objectivity regarding religious conflicts.</note> praised their dignified conduct and godly life with great excellence (*), which, however, could not prevent them from being attacked in that same year by a strong army in the Valleys, at the same time when the Reformed Congregations planted by them in *Calabria* <note>Waldensian communities in Southern Italy were brutally suppressed in 1560–1561 as part of the Counter-Reformation.</note> suffered great hardship. Some places experienced the Enemy’s fury, but the brave resistance offered to him caused him to look for an exit in many other places: at the very least, he did not achieve his aim, and in the following year, through the intercession of the gentle Duchess <note>Margaret of Valois, Duchess of Savoy, who was sympathetic to the Reformers.</note>, peace was granted to them. Those who had escaped the violent massacre committed in *Calabria* and fled to the Valleys, as well as those who were greatly impoverished by the war, needed foreign support this year: the famous *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential Reformer based in Geneva.</note> sent for this purpose letters of recommendation to various Princes of *Germany*, which moved the Elector of the *Palatinate* and the Duke of *Württemberg* to follow the example of the charitable *Swiss* and generously come to the aid of the needy *Waldensians*. Through this, they recovered somewhat, enabling them to better withstand a storm that arose four years later. The never-resting Pope and his vassals brewed a new grief for them, which was announced to them in the year 1565 in a strict Edict <term>Edict: A formal government proclamation or law, often used here to refer to religious restrictions.</term>: ,,namely, that whoever did not follow the orders of the ,,Roman—

### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...whoever did not wish to live according to the **Roman Church**, had to depart from the Duke’s states after the lapse of two months, for which each person was given a period of 10 days to deliberate, etc." This decree did not sooner reach the ears of the Electors of *Saxony* and the *Palatinate*, than they decided to send the excellent *Johannes Junius* <note>Johannes Junius (1525–1588) was a reformed diplomat and counselor to the Elector of the Palatinate.</note> as Ambassador to the Duke of *Savoy*, to work toward the revocation of this harsh Edict and to secure free religious exercise for the *Waldensians*. *Junius* behaved excellently in this embassy and departed from there satisfied with the Duke’s compliance; yet he was no sooner gone than the Clergy brewed new plots. His bold, learned, and emphatic writing so charmed me that I have read that beautiful letter with admiration more than once (*). *Emanuel Philibert* <note>Emanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy (1528–1580), known as "Iron Head." This, then, was the reason that the Waldensians, under the benevolent reign of ***Charles Emmanuel*** (who confirmed their liberties until the renowned year of 1655), remained more or less exposed to the cunning and destructive plots of the Monks sent out by the ***Inquisition***. ## CHAPTER VI.

*A brief Sketch of the Persecution, in the year 1655.*

The cause of the cruel persecution of that renowned year is sought by *Gilles* <note>Pierre Gilles, a Waldensian pastor and author of "Ecclesiastical History of the Reformed Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont."</note> in *Spain* and by *Boyer* <note>Pierre Boyer, a French writer who published a history of the Waldensians in 1691.</note> in *Rome*, but it seems to us that the first provocation arose in this manner (*). It is well known that in the year 1641, such an unheard-of massacre was committed by the Roman Catholics among the Protestants of *Ireland* that within a few months more than 200,000 people lost their lives <note>The author refers to the Irish Rebellion of 1641. The death toll of 200,000 was a common contemporary Protestant estimate, though modern historians place the number of deaths from violence much lower.</note>. Whether this persecution was instigated by the Pope by means of the Monks—claiming that by this they would perform a pleasing service to the head of the Church and, through the shedding of this blood, bypass Purgatory and sail straight to Heaven—or whether the Monks had managed the matter without the Pope’s knowledge; at the very least, that Roman leader did not fail on this occasion to use his *Nuncio* <note>A diplomatic representative of the Pope.</note>, *J. B. Rinuncinus* <note>Giovanni Battista Rinuccini (1592–1653), the Papal Nuncio to Ireland during the Confederate Wars.</note>, to exert every effort to seize the Kingdom of *Ireland* for himself, under the pretext of having an Apostolic right over the entire world and its Kingdoms. This attempt, which aroused the displeasure of *Charles* I, King of *England*, failed him and remained for a time unavenged. But *Cromwell*, having taken the Protectorship of the mighty *England* into his hands after *Charles's* death and raging with resentment over the wicked plots of the Pope, decided [to expel] a great number of Irishmen,

...to do with the **Waldensians**: and when they dispatched another delegation to **Turin**, and this group flattered themselves that they would find a hearing—to which end they were kept dangling with fair words <note>The Dutch idiom "op den tuil hield" implies being led on or kept busy with empty promises.</note>—the Duke's army of 15,000 men, under the command of the Count of **Pianezza** <note>Written as *Pinaffe* in the source; referring to Andrea Gastaldo, Marquis of Pianezza.</note>, entered the Valleys on the 17th of **April** <note>original: *Grasmaand*, or "Grass-month."</note> 1655. On the 24th of that month, the most horrific massacre was carried out, of which we shall later bring something to the reader’s attention from one of **Morland’s** <note>Sir Samuel Morland (1625–1695), the English diplomat sent by Oliver Cromwell to protest the massacre.</note> letters. After this operation, churches and houses were set on fire, and this land, which might be compared to **Goshen** <note>A biblical reference to the fertile land in Egypt granted to the Israelites; a place of plenty.</note>, now presented the appearance of a burning **Etna** <note>The famous active volcano in Sicily.</note>. **Léger** <note>Jean Léger (1615–1670), a Waldensian pastor and author of a seminal history of the massacre.</note> acknowledged (*) that long afterward—namely after the end of this rage and the conclusion of peace—he found the most miserable monuments of inhuman cruelty upon the high roads: young girls set naked on wooden stakes; children hacked into four pieces, with one part scattered here and another there; skulls crushed against the rocks; bodies without heads, arms, or legs; torsos hung from trees, from which the entrails had been torn and the chest opened, just as one does with slaughtered beasts; the skins of people, flayed alive, nailed against the windows of the Court in the **Lucerna** Valley, and a thousand other horrific sights.

Many of the **Waldensians**, seeing that such a fate was destined for them through the enemy’s treachery, took up arms under the leadership of two brave commanders, **Janavel** <note>Giosuè Janavel, a legendary resistance leader known as the "Lion of Rora."</note> and **Jayer** <note>Bartolomeo Jayer, a captain of the Waldensian militia.</note>, who in truth performed wonders and were the instruments in the hand of God for the preservation of the remainder. The Count of **Pianezza** <note>original: *Pinaſſe*; referring to Andrea Gastaldo, Marquis of Pianezza, the commander of the ducal troops.</note> burst with spite because of this, and thereafter attacked other places, murdering everyone he encountered; he captured the wife and three children of **Janavel** <note>Joshua Janavel (1617–1690), known as the "Lion of Rora," who led the Waldensian guerrilla resistance.</note> and threatened him that if he did not submit and renounce his **heresy**, he would burn them; yes, also that if he caught Janavel himself, he would inflict the most severe tortures and punishments upon him. To this, that courageous **Commander** sent word in reply: that no punishment, however heavy, and no torture, however barbaric, could ever bring him to the abjuration of his **Religion**: and if he burned his wife and children, then no more than their bodies would be consumed, while he would commend their souls into the hands of God, just as he surrendered his own to God, should it please Him that he fall into the hands of his executioners. Following this, this illustrious **Waldensian** performed several brave deeds, causing nearly all the **Irish** <note>The "Irish" refers to regiments of Irish Catholic soldiers who, having been exiled by Cromwell, served as mercenaries for the Duke of Savoy and were noted for their particular brutality during the massacres.</note> to fall by the sword; he was even shot through by a bullet, and it was thought for certain that he would lose his life thereby; however, through God’s singular goodness, he was healed within a short time and returned again to the fray. At this time, **Jean Léger** returned to the Valleys, who, along with **Michelin** <note>Barthélemy Michelini, another key leader of the Waldensian resistance.</note>, behaved as a courageous Commander during times of combat, and outside of those times, performed the **Office of the Ministry**. They were present at the stubborn battle at **Vachera** <note>La Vachera is a strategic mountain plateau and pass that served as a natural fortress for the Waldensian defenders.</note>, and the glorious victory achieved then was to be thanked, under the blessing of God, to the wise commands they gave during the struggle. Meanwhile, the bloodthirsty enemies did not cease to give free rein to their cruelty, and **Janavel** and his men continued day after day to achieve one victory or another.

After the sending of this so emphatic and Christian letter, which can give us a complete idea of the feelings and characters of our then-governors, Mr. van **Ommeren** departed for **Piedmont**. While awaiting the outcome of his **Embassy**, the **States General** <note>The federal governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> sent a letter to the States of the individual **Provinces**, requesting—after having given a soul-stirring account of the miserable condition of the **Waldensians**—that they would set a day, specifically the fifth of **September** <note>original: "Herfstmaand," literally 'Autumn-month,' an archaic Dutch term for September.</note>, to have a general **Collection** for the **Waldensians** held in all churches, both in the countryside and in the cities. Furthermore, they requested that the Ministers be exhorted to prepare and arrange their sermons and prayers in such a way that the people would be earnestly moved to give generous gifts for those poor and naked members of the mystical body of **Christ** <note>original: "verborgen lichaam," referring to the theological concept of the Church as the invisible or "hidden" body of Christ.</note>. Beyond this, a Day of Fasting and Prayer was to be held on that same day to plead for the continuation of God’s blessing and grace over the **Netherlands**. This request was heard with joy by all Provinces, and the aforementioned day was established. I may add here, to the honor of the Honorable Burgomasters of the as charitable as it is powerful and richly blessed **Amsterdam**, that those zealous city fathers instructed the Ministers of their city to give a short sketch of the misery of the **Waldensians** in their sermons the Sunday before, and further to inform the Congregation that on the appointed day, several Elders and Deacons would stand at the doors of the churches to receive alms; concluding their report to the Chur-

### OF THE WALDENSIANS. 43

Church Council sent for that purpose to present it to the Congregation, with these words: *hereby we pray and request the good Congregation of this blessed City, (since we still have bread in abundance) that they may then show the fruits of their charitable love, and thus meet the needs of our poor brothers; for it behooves us to take part in the affliction of Joseph <note>original: "de verbreekinge Josephs." A biblical reference to Amos 6:6, calling for empathy with the suffering of fellow believers.</note>, to weep with those who weep, to remember the prisoners as if we ourselves were imprisoned, and those who are ill-treated as if we also were ourselves ill-treated in the body, etc.*

Such solemn addresses had the desired influence on generous Netherlanders: exceptional gifts were given, which did not impoverish our ancestors, but rather made room to receive a new reward of grace from the hand of the ever-beneficent Godhead.

Let us now follow the Gentlemen *Morland* <note>Sir Samuel Morland (1625–1695), the English diplomat sent by Oliver Cromwell to protest the massacres of the Waldensians.</note> and *van Ommeren* <note>Casper van Ommeren, the diplomat representing the Dutch Republic on the same mission.</note> on their journey to the Valleys, where they will become eyewitnesses to the bloody slaughterhouses, and will find the sad remains of the murdered Valley-dwellers <note>original: "Dallieden." *Leger* was in *The Hague* when this happened, ready to travel to *England* to look after the interests of the *Waldensians*, when this unpleasant news reached his ears. The great esteem which this man had earned from the *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, the *Electors of Brandenburg* and the *Palatinate*, the *Landgrave of Hesse*, and the *Swiss Cantons*, moved these high Powers—knowing how useful *Leger* was to the *Valleys*—to send letters of recommendation to the *Duke of Savoy*.

The Council for the Propagation of the Faith, finding itself in a difficult position, managed to arrange matters at the Court so that *Leger* was permitted to come to the *Duke’s* territories to defend himself. He, having arrived in *Geneva* in the meantime for the sake of the *Waldensians*, easily understood how unsafe a defense in *Piedmont* would be for him; he therefore declined the proposal and, shortly thereafter, to the unspeakable grief of his old congregation, was called as a Minister to the Walloon Church <note>A French-speaking Protestant church in the Netherlands, often serving refugees from France and the Southern Netherlands.</note> in *Leiden*, which call he accepted and departed for that city. While there, he wrote his *History of the Waldensians* in *French*, looked after the interests of his countrymen until his death, and from time to time sent large sums of money, provided to him through *Dutch* charity, to the *Valleys*.

## CHAPTER VII.

*Containing the events from the year 1655 to 1672, and especially a heavy war in the year 1662.*

The Council for the Propagation of the Faith <term>Known in Latin as the *Congregatio de Propaganda Fide*, this committee in Turin was established to convert Protestants to Catholicism, often using political and military pressure.</term> of *Turin*, forgetting the sworn peace of the year 1655 and the promises solemnly made to the envoys of *England* and *Holland*, and now seeing that the *Waldensians* could not be brought down by force, took other paths that were no less dangerous than they were ungodly. This faithless Council held so little integrity in this weighty matter!

It first undertook to disturb the peace—so sweet to the *Waldensians* after the previous heavy persecutions—by bribing men who, for the sake of profit, allowed themselves to be used for all kinds of wicked enterprises. By means of these men, rumors were spread throughout the Valleys that the money collected in *Holland* and *England* <note>Following the massacres of 1655, Oliver Cromwell in England and the Dutch States General organized massive fundraising campaigns to support the surviving Waldensians.</note> was either being withheld by the distributors to enrich themselves, or was being distributed on an unequal footing, whereby some had received too much and others too little. The most trouble at this time was stirred up by a *Jesuit* <term>A member of the Society of Jesus, a Catholic order often viewed with deep suspicion by Protestants as being deceptive spies for the Counter-Reformation.</term> named *Longueil*, who pretended to come from *Languedoc* <note>A province in southern France.</note>, claiming to have renounced the *Roman* religion there and being very eager to live henceforth in the Valleys among the *Waldensians*. This "wolf" having skillfully clothed himself in "sheep's clothing," managed to so thoroughly charm the simple and unsuspecting *Waldensians* that they entrusted him with the management of the school at *Villars*. ...[The delegates were] granted twelve days, which were thereafter extended so long that Peace was struck on the 14th of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaand," an archaic Dutch name for February</note> 1664, and the *Waldensians* were restored to their old privileges and the free exercise of their Religion.

With uncommon joy, these Valley-people <note>original: "Dallieden," referring to the inhabitants of the Waldensian valleys</note> returned to the cultivation of their lands and the observance of public worship, forgetting their recent troubles, until new ones arose and made them wary of the consequences. The Council for the Propagation of the Faith <term>Raad ter Geloofsvoortplanting: the local branch of the *Congregatio de Propaganda Fide*, a Vatican institution established to counter the spread of Protestantism</term>, unable to bear this peace, twisted itself into all manner of turns to transform the Peace so solemnly sworn by the Duke into new theaters of war. One could hardly believe what inventions were devised for this purpose, and it would have been impossible to protect oneself against such great wickedness and subtleties if the all-governing God, *in whose hand the heart of Kings and Princes is as streams of water* <note>A reference to Proverbs 21:1: "The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."</note>, had not inclined the mind of Duke *Charles Emmanuel* toward favoring the *Waldensians* and turned the counsels of their enemies into foolishness. This Prince, who did not lack judgment, having accurately investigated the conduct of the *Waldensians*, found that people had tried to make them hateful to him without cause. Remembering with what zeal they had served him on various occasions, and particularly how faithfully they had stood by him during a rebellion in the years 1638 and 1640, he decided not to begin any hostilities against them.

Thus our Brethren and fellow believers enjoyed eight years of rest—and oh, if only this and all other Dukes of *Savoy* had always seen with their own eyes and never lent an ear to the persecutory counsels of the Council for the Propagation of the Faith!

At *Tailleret*, the enemy was repelled most courageously. Those who attacked the *Waldensians* at *Angrogne* could not make them yield a foot’s breadth, but had to retreat with heavy losses. Those of *St. Germain*, not being on their guard because of the truce and busy gathering provisions, suffered the heaviest blow and escaped by flight; however, the treacherous enemy gained little by this shameful deed. The *Waldensians*, overflowing with joy that they—though not yet 700 men strong—had held back an army of 18,000 soldiers and, with the loss of only six men, had killed 1,500 enemies (among whom were prominent commanders), offered honor and thanksgiving to God for this great victory.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *The fortunes of the Waldensians from the year 1672 to 1687, including one of the most severe Persecutions, along with their expulsion from the Valleys of Piedmont.*

In the famous year 1672, when William III, Prince of Orange—who would later become an eminent Protector of the *Waldensians*—first took to the field in the Netherlands, recaptured three provinces already seized by France, and restored our ancestors' freedom, the *Waldensians* did not fight to protect their own Valleys. However, as the Duke had declared war on the Genoese, they were obliged to give proof of their loyalty and obedience to him. Having learned to render unto Caesar what is Caesar’s, and unto God what is God’s <note>A reference to the biblical command in Matthew 22:21 regarding civic duty and religious devotion.</note>, they donned their armor, reinforced his Army, marched with him, and served him with such zeal and bravery that he not only highly praised their military courage and unshaken loyalty in letters (*) written to them, but also assured them of his protection and favor forever, which he honored until his death, which occurred in the year 1678. His widow, the Duchess Regent <note>Marie Jeanne Baptiste of Savoy-Nemours, who ruled as regent for her son, Victor Amadeus II.</note>, being not ignorant of these matters, treated them on equal footing after his death; and what is more, she committed herself to the Swiss in the year 1679 to maintain the *Waldensians* in their privileges and free exercise of Religion at all times.

# CHURCH HISTORY

In the year 1685, the Governor of the Valleys, by order of the Duke—who had been urged to do so by the King of *France*—proclaimed under heavy penalty that all foreigners, namely the Reformed who had fled from neighboring *France* <note>These were Huguenots fleeing the increasing persecution under Louis XIV.</note>, must depart the Valleys within three days, and that no one was permitted to harbor them. Despite the heavy storm this small rising cloud seemed to predict for the *Waldensians*, they continued to live in relative peace after the departure of these refugees, until the storm suddenly burst over their heads.

*Victor Amadeus II*, a young Prince of good intellect and princely qualities, who was always very averse to all persecutions and cruelties, had until now not been able to bring himself to do more at France's request than to refuse shelter to the French refugees in the Valleys. However, *Louis XIV*, having decided upon a total extermination of the Reformed and noticing *Victor's* reluctance and displeasure regarding this, had his envoy, Rebenac Feuquieres, deliver this threatening declaration to the Duke on a certain day:

> "that the King, his Master, if the Duke
> of Savoy remained unwilling, would certainly find
> means to banish the Heretics from the Val-
> leys with 14,000 men, and would then
> keep the Valleys for himself."

This fierce threat from the powerful *Louis*, given further weight by the Council for the Propagation of the Faith <note>The *Congregatio de Propaganda Fide*, a Catholic administrative body dedicated to spreading Catholicism and suppressing Protestantism.</note>, made the young Duke waver.

### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

Between the two, he had to choose: either lose his states or force the *Waldensians* to adopt the Roman religion. It is easy to understand which way a Catholic-leaning Prince, unable to withstand Louis's overwhelming power, would lean in such a case. He chose the latter, and subsequently, on the 31st of January <note>Original: *Louwmaand*, an old Dutch name for the month of January.</note> in the year 1686, he had this command proclaimed in the Valleys:

> “that the free exercise
> of religion shall henceforth no longer take
> place, under threat of the death penalty and
> forfeiture of property for the unwill-
> ing—that the churches of the *Waldensians* be demolished
> and the Ministers henceforth be ban-
> ished—that the children be baptized, raised in the Roman
> religion, and any refusing
> parents shall be sentenced to the Galleys <note>A form of grueling forced labor as rowers on naval vessels, often resulting in death from exhaustion or maltreatment.</note>.”

No one can express the desolation of the *Waldensians* upon the proclamation of this decree by the Duke. They saw themselves plunged into an abyss of misery that was terrifying and offered not the slightest glimmer of hope for deliverance. The joyful light of the Gospel, which had shone among them for so many centuries since the time of the Apostles, now threatened to go out forever, and their children were to be forced into accepting a doctrine that they had opposed for centuries. Mistreated Christians! Wretched people! One might say, how powerfully you experience the truth of Jesus’s prediction: *In the world you shall have tribulation.* <note>A reference to John 16:33.</note> What could be done in such a thorny situation? Humble petitions submitted to the gracious Duke carried no weight due to the aforementioned political reasons. Louis XIV, who until this point had been their protector and advocate <note>Louis XIV had previously acted as a mediator for the Waldensians during the massacres of 1655, making his current role as their persecutor a bitter betrayal.</note>, now laid the first foundation for their ruin and, to that end, already had an army marching toward them. <note>(*) The Duke of *Savoy* was at that time effectively a vassal of *France*.</note>

The *Swiss* Envoys, realizing that the *Waldensians*, lacking commanders and well-organized military bands, were no match for the war powers of *France* and *Savoy*, and consequently that nothing better could be devised than for them to leave their Fatherland and look for a safe haven, had this proposal made to the *Waldensians*. They found this matter to be of such great weight that they called for a general assembly to consider this harsh condition. The *Swiss* Envoys then requested a safe-conduct pass for some *Waldensians* who might bring them the results of the assembly, which the *Turinese* Court refused. Necessity then forced them to send their Secretary to *Angrogne*, who found the *Waldensians* there to be very divided. ...sufficiently learned that their total destruction had been decided upon, [they] resolved after the proclamation not to accept the offered freedom, but to follow the example of their Fathers, and to commend the outcome of their cause to Divine Providence: thus this Proclamation <note>original: *Placaat*; a formal public decree or edict issued by a sovereign authority.</note>, designed to divide them among themselves, now served to bring about their general union.

And indeed, how could they resolve to tear down their Churches, dedicated to the Most High God, with their own hands, according to the demand of that Proclamation; to lay down their weapons; to throw open their Fatherland to Priests and Monks; to surrender themselves to an army of soldiers which would escort them outside their Fatherland; fearing—not without reason, as the outcome later taught—that the latter was only a cover to suddenly finish them off as defenseless victims at the hands of bloodthirsty soldiers.

They sent this decision to the Swiss Envoys and begged them to insist on better terms: yet nothing was to be obtained as long as they remained under arms. This was clear proof that the intent was to disarm them, and then to destroy them without a blow. They then took the resolution to defend themselves against all attack, in which they were strengthened by the following occurrence. Three days after the proclamation of the Decree, some *Waldensians*, intending to depart, went to request safe-conduct <term>safe-conduct|A formal document or guarantee of protection allowing someone to travel through a dangerous or hostile area.</term> from the Governor: yet under the pretext that they could not leave alone, but must wait until the others also departed, this was refused to them. And meanwhile, others were thrown [into prison], whom they had in vain [tried] to embrace...

In this general distress, a general assembly was held on the 19th of April <note>original: *Grasmaand*; an old Dutch name for the month of April, literally meaning "grass month."</note> at Rocheplatte, in which they all resolved to remain in the Valleys, and that all Ministers would preach the following Lord’s Day according to the circumstances of matters and times, and distribute the Lord’s Supper.

Meanwhile, the Duke took to the field and held a review of his army on a plain at the foot of the *Alps*, intending to attack the Valleys once the eight days specified in the Proclamation for laying down arms had ended. The *Waldensians*, nearly 2,500 men strong, entrenched themselves as well as they could—as a people without Commanders and inexperienced in military science are accustomed to doing in times of need, and consequently not without mistakes. One of these was the desire to defend all their posts at once, only abandoning the outermost ones in case of dire need, and only then strengthening themselves upon the mountains.

On the 22nd of April, the day destined for the attack, the French Army, under the command of *Catinat* <note>Nicolas Catinat (1637–1712), a prominent French military commander and later Marshal of France.</note>, Governor of *Casal*, marched toward the Valleys of *Perouse* and *St. Martin* two hours before dawn by torchlight; a portion of the Army attacked the entrenchments of the *Waldensians* at *St. Germain*, and being six times stronger than their opponents, the enemies did not expect to be repulsed, which nevertheless happened: having to retreat with heavy loss after the attack, the *Waldensians* fell upon them, and they, not expecting such a bold deed, were driven back into the plain of *Cluson* <note>The Chisone valley (French: *Cluson*), located in the Piedmont region.</note>, with a loss of 500 men, according to their own admission, while the

This promise was poorly kept, for after the surrender, they were all taken prisoner and brought to *Luserna* <note>original: Lucern; the main town in the Val Pellice</note>, under the pretext that they had to solemnly submit to the Duke there. Thereupon, a dehumanized rage against women and children was given free rein: the wanton soldiers committed such acts of unheard-of cruelty and immorality that shame forbids us to grant them a place in this narrative.

The darkness of the approaching night favored the flight and escape of some, who shortly thereafter sent word to *Don Gabriel* <note>Don Gabriel of Savoy (1673–1699), the illegitimate son of Duke Charles Emmanuel II and commander in the Piedmontese army.</note> requesting him to cease hostilities and to set their imprisoned brothers free, but he did not deign to send back an answer.

After this victory, or rather after this treacherous conduct, the enemies captured the remaining posts and then declared that anyone who would apostatize and become *Roman* <note>original: Roomfch; meaning to convert to Roman Catholicism</note> would be restored to the free possession of his dwelling and goods.

Many other *Waldensians*, not yet informed of this, also relied on the good faith of the enemies and the offer of forgiveness made to them: yet they were treated like the previous ones: old and young, the ministers not excepted, were taken prisoner, bound, and dragged away, and whoever could not follow was pushed down from the highest rocky cliffs, so that their bodies, crashing with great force onto the lower rocks, were torn asunder, and their limbs remained hanging in the branches of the trees below.

But let us first examine how they had been treated in those dungeons since their surrender.

It is a difficult task to provide a true depiction of the misery endured for nine months in those prisons. Imagine 12,000 people—men, women, and children alike—locked within fourteen cramped prisons, treated according to whatever small measure of mercy their jailers <term>Cipiers</term> <note>Prison wardens or guards.</note> might have retained. Some provided the prisoners with only bread and water; others threw them foul black bread kneaded with muddy water scooped from street gutters, in which glass, lime, or stones were often found. Some were given stinking water to these wretched souls, and others were forced to fetch it from the filthy troughs from which the livestock drank. It was given to them only at fixed hours of the day, and not when they were thirsty, a practice that caused many to die. They were forced to sleep on hard planks without straw, or, if a jailer wished to lay them more softly, they were given rotten straw. The prisons were so crowded for such a multitude that they could scarcely move; whenever someone died—which happened daily—another was immediately put in their place. The stifling summer heat, the damp, unventilated rooms, and the lack of clean linen caused the vermin <note>Primarily lice and fleas, which spread typhus and other "jail fevers."</note> to multiply violently, tormenting the prisoners day and night and robbing them of sleep. Some were even eaten by worms, and the outer skin of their bodies rotted away. In this wretched state, these sufferers were left to lie until—

They were refused candles—a comfort so pleasant and inexpensive during the long winter evenings—so that when the sun rose late and set early, they lived mostly in darkness. The sick could obtain no compassion and therefore died without medicines, relief, or care. Sometimes they were taken to open places where they were exposed to all the hardships of the weather, the fury of the winds, and the cold of the snow: a cruelty that was almost "charitable" <note>The author uses irony here, suggesting that the cruelty of exposure was a mercy because it killed the prisoners faster, ending their suffering.</note> because it rarely failed to bring a speedy end to their miserable lives and exchange them for eternity. Women in childbirth <term>Kraamvrouwen</term> were denied the assistance of midwives <term>Vroedvrouwen</term>, which resulted in their own deaths and the deaths of their children at the very moment they began to live. Charitable people who, moved by such great misery, wished to bring some soft food to the sick were driven away from the prisons; and anyone who dared to complain about this or that rough treatment was forced into silence by insults and blows with a stick. Let me bring these tragic scenes <note>Original: "treurtoneelen," literally "theater of mourning" or "tragedy."</note> to an end—though only a rough sketch of this inhumane treatment has been given—and state that they had been brought into this wretched condition when the Duke of *Savoy* <term>Savoye</term> <note>Victor Amadeus II (1666–1732). This was a mercy that the *Swiss* envoys, as mentioned earlier, had secured from the Count of *Govon* <note>Count Giuseppe Govone, a diplomat and official in the Savoyard court.</note>.

This release proceeded in the following manner: Some of those who, in moments of overwhelming despair <term>moedeloosheid</term>, had promised to change their religion, were not permitted to remain in *Piedmont* <term>Piemont</term>, because their promises, made under duress, were deemed to have no force. Although others were allowed to apostatize <term>afval</term> <note>The act of renouncing one's faith, in this case, converting to Catholicism to escape death.</note>, they were not restored to their homes as promised, but were instead led away as captives to the Domain of *Vercelli* (*), the most barren part of *Piedmont*. The children, scattered here and there, upon hearing of the release of their parents and not wanting to leave them, were held back by force; so too were other prisoners to whom the Duke's order had not been announced, even though it encompassed a general liberation.

Since more than 8,000 had died in prison from the wretchedness, while few had renounced their faith, and the children along with some others were held back, no more than 3,000 *Waldensians* departed in the winter month <note>December.</note> of the year 1686: a pitiful remnant of so many brave people! these—

Let me bring these tragic scenes to an end—although only a rough sketch of this inhuman treatment has been given—and say that they had been brought to this wretched state when the Duke of Savoy <note>Victor Amadeus II (1666–1732), who persecuted the Waldensians under pressure from King Louis XIV of France.</note>, undoubtedly ignorant of their miserable condition (as people were accustomed to hide it from him as much as possible), gave the order to release them and have them depart for Switzerland. This was a kindness that the Swiss Envoys, as mentioned above, had obtained from the Count of Govon <note>Count Giuseppe Govone.</note>.

This release proceeded as follows: Some of those who, in moments of irresistible despondency, had promised to change their religion <note>Meaning they had agreed to convert to Roman Catholicism to escape torture or death.</note>, were not allowed to stay in Piedmont, because their promises made in distress were considered to have no legal force. Furthermore, although others were permitted to apostatize <note>To renounce their Protestant faith.</note>, they were not restored to their homes as had been promised; instead, they were led away as prisoners to the Lordship of Vercelli (*), the most infertile part of Piedmont. The children, who were scattered here and there, hearing of their parents' release and not wishing to leave them, were held back by force. The same happened to other prisoners to whom the Duke's order had not been announced, even though it involved a general release.

Because more than 8,000 had died in prison through sheer misery, and a few had apostatized, and the children with some others were held back, no more than 3,000 Waldensians departed in the winter month <note>This refers to December.</note> of the year 1686: a pitiful remnant of so many brave people! these

### OF THE WALDENSES.

After one troop after another had arrived here, a change was seen in this mournful spectacle. Everyone here was equally anxious to hear something of their kinsmen and friends. 

This mournful display was completed by the bitter reports with which the general curiosity, alas, was all too well satisfied. The hope—the idle hope of many women—that their husbands (from whom they had been separated while locked in different prisons) still lived, vanished suddenly through the testimony of others who had seen them succumb to misery and die by their side in prison. ### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...and villages of the Canton of Bern. Here they earned their living partly by the labor of their hands, and were partly supported by the large sums of money sent over from England and Holland <note>This refers to the extensive relief funds raised by Protestant allies; in England, Oliver Cromwell had initiated a "Great Collection," and later, William III of Orange provided significant financial backing for the refugees.</note>. In this place, they enjoyed every freedom among their fellow believers and the finest opportunity to serve God and hear His word; so much so that they found nothing but complete contentment in these safe shelters. Yet, just as nothing on earth is perfect, it must be said that their condition—however different from their previous state in the prisons—remained unsettled. The desire for their Fatherland constantly pricked them, and who would wonder at this, having ever felt what it is to be driven from one’s own country against one's will and to have to wander abroad as an exile. The prevailing passion for the land of our birth, which the wise Creator has implanted in all nations for weighty reasons, gave them unrest in the midst of the greatest peace. These thoughts drifted so incessantly through their minds that they never ceased to wish, whatever the cost, to return to the place where they had first received life.

This humble beginning—this longing for their old dwellings found in a defenseless and banished people—may appear vain and ridiculous to the reader, because there was no probability whatsoever that this desire could ever be satisfied or such a goal achieved on any solid ground. Let us, however, examine the effects of this longing, all the more because they will open to us more pleasant scenes than the previous narrative and will gloriously bring to light the exceptional care that God has taken for the restoration of this poor people.
