## CHURCH HISTORY

Many times they consulted with one another over this weighty matter. Who can believe that they, living here in such rest and peace through the kind care of the praiseworthy Cantons <note>The sovereign states of the Swiss Confederacy.</note>, still harbored the intention to return to a land where they had suffered so much? A land where thousands of remaining monuments <note>In this context, "monuments" refers to the physical reminders of their trauma, such as ruined homes and the graves of those killed during the massacres.</note> of their murdered friends would fill them with sorrow day after day and pierce their hearts miserably? Who could believe, however, that they went about this so casually, or that they had barely considered the nearly insurmountable difficulties? Yet these and many other obstacles could not extinguish their longing to return. Was this stubbornness, a reckless madness, or an arrangement of the secretly working Providence of the Almighty God?

The unquenchable love for their Fatherland was not revealed in the harboring of this hope alone, but it broke through all counter-arguments on this point and was finally made manifest through three devised and attempted means, of which the first two failed.

The first undertaking was begun without commanders, weapons, or other necessary preparations, although without these they could never have achieved a successful outcome. It was therefore their good fortune that this ill-conceived enterprise was halted at the very start. Having made themselves ready to return to their Valleys <note>The "Waldensian Valleys" in the Piedmont region of the Alps, where the community had lived for centuries before their expulsion.</note> and being on the verge of embarking at *Ouchi* <note>Now Ouchy, the port district of Lausanne on the shores of Lake Geneva.</note>, the Bailiff <note>A regional administrative official representing the ruling city-state.</note> of *Lausanne* commanded them, in the name of the Honorable Government of *Bern*, that everyone should return to his residence. They obeyed this order, though not without the pain of their failed attempt.

This first undertaking ended quietly, fortunately for them, without making much noise; however, the preparations for a second, better planned some time later, were subsequently also better executed. ### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...since they were no burden to the *Swiss*, [their stay] was permitted; *England* sent these unfortunates much assistance, and *Holland* alone transferred 24,000 *Ecus* <note>The Écu was a high-value silver or gold coin; 24,000 represented a very substantial relief fund for the era.</note>, which *William III*, Prince of *Orange* <note>William III of Orange-Nassau, who was both the Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland.</note>, had distributed among them through Mr. *Convenant*, formerly a Councilor of the Principality of *Orange*.

Once the winter had passed, they began to think of departing, yet the miserable exiles did not yet know where to go. Nothing pleased them less than traveling to *America*, which some had recommended. The Elector of *Brandenburg* <note>Frederick III, the Elector of Brandenburg and later the first King of Prussia, who was known for welcoming Protestant refugees.</note> offered his own land under advantageous conditions, in which they had no interest, whether due to the great distance, the foreign language, or the climate. Remaining without a firm decision and still in uncertainty, people began to regard them as stubborn individuals with whom no dealings could be made. This went so far that the *Swiss* ministers began to criticize these exiles in their public sermons, and the government of the *Cantons* <note>The sovereign states that make up the Swiss Confederation.</note>, displeased by so many advantageous conditions being rejected, now forced them to sign a promise to depart with their own hand. *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and soldier who led the Waldensians during their exile and eventual "Glorious Return" to their valleys.</note> was also among those who signed it, yet did not fail to protest this action, saying: that in this manner they were being coerced; but nothing could be done against it.

Eight hundred *Waldensians*, both men and women, then prepared for the journey to *Brandenburg* and set off for *Frankfurt am Main*, receiving safe passage everywhere throughout the states of *Germany*. In the aforementioned city, a *Secretary* of the Elector came to meet them, to then escort them to *Berlin*, where they were received with affection by that magnanimous Prince, and were thereafter distributed and cared for within his lands.

# ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

...to be, in spite of all the advantages granted to them by the last Duke, and the new offers made by the Duke of *Wurttemberg* <note>Original: *Wirtemberg*.</note>, to vacate his land, leave their half-built dwellings, and thus once again escape the hands of their enemies. But now the old difficulty surfaced again: where to go now after so much struggling? In *Switzerland* they could expect no warm welcome; to penetrate deeper into *Germany* would bring about their certain downfall. Tossed by a thousand thoughts, the All-ruling God <note>The Dutch *Albestierende God* emphasizes God's total sovereignty over human affairs.</note> inspired them to seek out their first place of refuge—that is, to return to *Switzerland*, regardless of what might come of it.

Let us be permitted here to pause our narrative for a moment and, in this place, reflect upon the wonderful ways of God with this poor people. *France* had previously been the first and only cause of them being driven from their Fatherland; but now, by God’s secret decree, *France* becomes the primary means of bringing them back to their old dwellings. Thus, all things here must work together for the good of these exiles <note>A reference to the biblical promise in Romans 8:28.</note>. Oh, that the world might at all times take heed of the instructive Providence and Governance of God, and gather wisdom therefrom!

Let us return with the traveling *Waldenses* to *Switzerland* to see what befell them there. The *Swiss*, having not failed to keep an eye on them incessantly out of brotherly love, had to acknowledge the good intentions of the *Waldenses* in settling in a foreign land. They knew how far they had already advanced their heavy labor, which lands they had sown, and which houses they had begun to build: because of this, [forgetting] the previous displeasure...

### OF THE WALDENSIANS

...living, they received them once again with open arms. One Canton persuaded the other to readmit these exiles and provide them with shelter; all the more so because they were not led astray by laziness, nor did they wish to live on the alms of others, but earned their keep with their own hands. And on this occasion, we must not forget to mention that since their expulsion from the Valleys, never more than a single complaint regarding misconduct has been heard. In *Zurich* <note>A major Swiss city and key center of the Protestant Reformation that provided significant aid to the Waldenses.</note>, a *Waldensian soldier* had at one time taken a weapon from his master, but as soon as this became known to one of the leaders, he did not rest until it was returned to the owner.

Having returned to charitable *Switzerland*, they were given rest, time, and opportunity to consider why they had undergone such many and long-lasting calamities: why they had been tossed back and forth by so many adversities. After ripe reflections, they reached this conclusion: that they had too much forgotten their dear Fatherland, which is why God had not wished to grant them rest until now; and they firmly established that God would never give them rest until they sought out the Land of their Birth again, and there relit the extinguished light of the Gospel <note>This refers to the Waldensian motto, *Lux Lucet in Tenebris* ("The Light Shines in the Darkness"). The "light" symbolizes their preservation of what they considered the pure, original Christian faith.</note>.

This plan was then resumed, and they were encouraged in it not a little by the homecoming of the spies whom they had sent out a year ago, as mentioned above. These now brought back this joyful news: that the Duke's <note>Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy, whose troops had occupied the Waldensian valleys.</note> troops had left the Mountains at the beginning of the year 1689 and had withdrawn, whether because that Prince [had moved his forces elsewhere]...

...thirdly, that he no longer feared the *Waldensians*, or that he needed his troops against those of *Mondovi* <note>Mondovì is a town in the Piedmont region; the Duke was dealing with local uprisings known as the "Salt Wars" around this time.</note>.

Hardly can one imagine what joyful news this brought to them, which was also not a little increased by the great and happy change that occurred in *England* at this time. *William III*, Prince of Orange and Stadtholder of the *Netherlands*, seeing that the liberty of that Kingdom and the Reformed Religion <note>The Protestant faith as practiced by the followers of Calvin and other reformers.</note> were going to ruin due to the poor governance of King *James II*—to whose daughter, the incomparable *Mary*, he was married—and being strongly urged by the *English* nation to cross over with a fleet of ships for their deliverance, undertook this weighty matter with the counsel of the States-General of the *Netherlands*. Thereupon, within three days, he hired 500 transport ships to carry the *Dutch* troops across, and set out from the *Dutch* harbors into the sea on the 19th of October <note>original: "Wynmaand" — the traditional Dutch name for October, the "wine month."</note> 1688 with this great fleet, landing shortly after at *Torbay*. King *James* then fled the kingdom, and the *English* nation bestowed the crowns of that realm upon that excellent Prince and his Princess *Mary*, whereby *England's* liberty and religion were completely restored.

From this revolution of affairs, *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud was a pastor and the primary military leader of the Waldenses during their "Glorious Return."</note> promised himself much good. He knew what this Prince, while still in *Holland*, had said to him and had, in any case, promised him his powerful protection, upon which he could safely rely, not having to deal with a fickle monarch. From *William’s* zeal for the Reformed Religion, from his alliance with the *Protestant* princes of *Europe*, and from *England’s* aversion to *France*, he could expect nothing but joyful consequences for the benefit of the *Waldensians*.

He further foresaw that England would shortly have to declare war against *France*, as indeed happened soon after, and understood that this war would be waged by the brave *William* <note>William III of Orange, recently crowned King of England, who was a champion of the Protestant cause against French hegemony.</note> in person. This would give *Louis XIV* <note>Louis XIV of France, known as the "Sun King," whose persecution of the Huguenots and expansionist wars made him the primary antagonist of the Waldensians.</note> so much work that the great Monarch would not look toward him and his small bands. If ever, he now judged the time and the right opportunity to be ripe to drop the mask and make use of this auspiciously favorable moment. He had learned from the failures of the first two undertakings that the lack of secrecy regarding their intentions was the true cause of their poor outcomes. 

When he then revealed his great and weighty objective to the Leaders of the *Waldensians*, and found them all inclined toward the undertaking—for he was not only their Pastor <note>original: "Leeraar" — literally "teacher," but used here to denote his role as their spiritual minister.</note>, but also their sole commander-in-chief—he insisted above all else that this new Plan must be kept secret with the utmost care. This was so that the difficult passage through mountainous *Savoy*, which was now open, would not be blocked should their intentions leak out; and so that the Government of *Bern* <note>The Swiss city-state of Bern was providing refuge to the Waldensians but was diplomatically pressured by the Duke of Savoy to prevent them from launching a counter-attack from Swiss soil.</note>, bound by treaty with the Duke to prevent their departure, would neither take measures to contest their aims, nor later be exposed to the Duke's reproaches once they carried out their design. And indeed, they made their arrangements so cautiously and wisely that the common *Waldensians*, at their command, prepared themselves for the journey without knowing where they were going.

## CHAPTER X.

### *Preparations for the recapture of the Valleys, undertaken by the Waldensians.*

These were the beginnings of the third undertaking, in the Summer of the year 1689, which by the wondrous guidance of Providence <note>The Waldensians frequently attributed their survival and military successes to "Providence," reflecting their belief that they were a chosen people protected by God.</note> met with success. We come now to a renowned journey, a perilous enterprise, not to be begun except by those driven by an exceeding love for their Fatherland and an all-conquering, pure zeal for the restoration of their uprooted Religion. We begin with the account of a momentous matter, carried out gloriously by a handful of People—trusting in the justice of their cause and in that God whose they were and whom they served—to the astonishment of all *Europe*, with unyielding heroism and amidst the endurance of the most extreme dangers.

Having deliberated upon everything, they mutually agreed to choose the *Woods of Nyon* (*) as a general gathering place, and to depart for that location at an appointed time. That place was indeed well-conceived and very well suited to their purpose. Nowhere could they remain more hidden or be more easily provided with provisions. Here they were near *Lake Geneva*, where they could be embarked in all silence in the dead of night and be set ashore on the opposite side in the *Duchy of Savoy* <note>The Duchy of Savoy was the Waldensians' homeland, but at this time it was hostile territory under the rule of Victor Amadeus II, who had exiled them under pressure from France.</note>.

(*) This Wood is found between *Nyon* and *Rolle*, two small Towns on *Lake Geneva*.

Being rightly and highly fearful of being discovered, they decided together to make a virtue of necessity and to cross the *Lake of Geneva* <note>original: "Geneeffche Meir"</note> without the others. *Arnaud*, having set foot on Land first with 14 *Waldenses* between Nernier (*) and Yvoire, two Villages of the Duchy of Chablais in *Savoy*, immediately stationed sentries at the access roads to avoid being surprised while his People were disembarked. The new General <note>original: "Veldheer," referring to Henri Arnaud</note> then made a second division: he assigned some to the vanguard, others to the *main body* <note>original: "corps de bataille"</note>, and some to the rearguard. This was a formation used by regular military units, which he followed with the utmost caution and—as will soon be seen—applied at the right time for his own preservation and success. After these and some other necessary preparations, they were all ready for the journey.

Besides *Arnaud*, whom one might call their Patriarch, Teacher, and General, there were two other ministers in this small army, *Chyon* and *Montoux*. These men now had the travel-ready *Waldensians* kneel upon the ground so that, before setting foot forward, they might pray to *Heaven* for Divine favor and assistance for their great undertaking. Having performed this solemn and dignified act, *Chyon* went ahead to the first village to seek a guide. Had his purpose not been discovered, as he did not suspect it was, he would have easily obtained one from the inhabitants. However, to his misfortune, a *Savoyard* nobleman had spotted the *Waldensians* on the shore of the Lake <note>Lake Geneva (Lac Léman), which the Waldensians crossed to begin their trek.</note> and immediately threw all the villagers into an uproar with a call to arms. Thus, when *Chyon* arrived there, he was stopped and taken prisoner, later transported to *Chambery*, and held in confinement until the conclusion of the peace treaty. Instead of *Chyon* returning as expected, the aforementioned nobleman appeared, armed with pistols in hand, to scout the area, as it were. *Arnaud*, spotting him, approached him with several *Waldensians*. Seeing this, the nobleman fled, and as they pursued him and moved further ahead, they

## OF THE WALDENSIANS.

...found everything discovered and the villagers in alarm.

After a short consultation, *Arnaud* sent some men ahead and had the inhabitants told, under strong threats, to lay down their arms and grant them free passage. These villagers, not daring to offer resistance, remained quiet and let him pass through; but he, not trusting them, took two guides and some hostages with him for his safety, who, however, were released shortly thereafter in a polite manner as soon as he had obtained others along the way.

Thus this small army marched onward fairly calmly, yet very much on its guard, with *Arnaud* maintaining such strict and precise military discipline <term>military discipline: original "krygstugt," referring to the rigorous conduct Arnaud demanded to ensure his men acted as a professional army rather than a lawless mob</term> everywhere, that the peasants, drawn out by this, came forward with their priests to watch them pass by. Some, understanding their purpose, wished them success; others called out to them: *God be with you!* <note>original: "God zy met u!"</note> The priest of *Filli* <note>Likely the village of Fillinges in the Savoy region.</note> offered them some refreshments.

Having advanced for some time, the vanguard stopped four *Savoyard* noblemen on horseback. They wanted to speak with the commanders of the *Waldensians*, to ask the reason for this action, and to command them to lay down their arms; but the vanguard answering that they had no right to ask such questions, they judged it best—upon seeing the main body of the army following—to take flight.

The vanguard prevented this, made them dismount, and forced them to march in the first ranks as prisoners as punishment for their audacity <note>original: "stoutheid," meaning their impudent attempt to command an armed force</note>.

The army now arrived at a mountain, and having crossed it, they discovered near a forest two hundred peasants in arms, under the leadership of two gentlemen, *Gropel* and *Mouche*, who were in the service of the Duke of *Savoy*, and [had heard] this quickly spreading rumor that the *Waldensians* had entered the country,

At midnight, they came to a small mountain, where they halted in an open field called *Carman*, to catch their breath after a long and continuous march—even though it was raining a little—and to wait for daybreak, so they might cross the Bridge of *Marni*, which they had heard was broken, without hindrance. II. Day, a day of prosperity.

*Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor who led the Waldensians on their military trek to reclaim their Piedmontese valleys.</note> found the Bridge of *Marni* <note>The bridge at Marigny over the Arve river.</note> with his army, to his great joy, in good condition, and crossed it immediately without meeting any resistance; he then descended into a pleasant valley, which had been deserted by the peasants on account of the approaching *Waldensians*. At six o'clock in the morning, he approached to within a musket-shot of the beautifully fortified town of *Clufe* <note>Modern Cluses.</note>, which he had to pass through. Since the fortifications were occupied by armed inhabitants upon their arrival, *Arnaud* decided to prepare for an attack; however, one of the hostages, fearing death if this undaunted army were held back, requested permission to write a letter to the town government to obtain an unhindered passage. This was granted to him. After some deliberation and questioning of a *Waldensian* commander by the government as to where his authority <note>original: "bevel" (order or commission)</note> was, he replied: *at the point of my sword* <note>original: "aan de punt van myn deegen"</note>. The government, seeing that he was in earnest, decided to allow the passage on the condition that everything they took with them would be paid for. The armed citizens then lined up in rows along the streets, the gates were opened, and *Arnaud* marched through with his army, paying 5 Louis d'ors <term>Louis d'ors: French gold coins named after King Louis XIII</term> for wine and bread that his men took with them, with which the townspeople were very satisfied. At the last gate they exited, he left a *detachment* <note>original: "Commando"</note> to cover the retreat, and here he showed signs that he could have become as great a General <term>General: original "Veldheer," a high-ranking military commander</term>—had he been raised in the trade of arms early on—as he already was a capable Teacher <term>Teacher: original "Leeraar," here referring to Arnaud's primary vocation as a Protestant minister</term>.

->### OF THE WALDENSIANS.<-

After leaving Cluse <note>Modern Cluses, a town in the Faucigny region of Savoy.</note>, they headed for Salanche (*); on the way, they discovered a servant of a certain Lord of Cluse who was traveling with them. Some, suspecting him of ill intent, seized him and found letters on him from the people of Cluse to the Government of Salanche, advising them to take up arms and hold back the Waldensians long enough so that they <note>The people of Cluse.</note> could attack them from the rear. Rejoicing at this discovery, they ensured the servant could never deliver these letters. 

Now they were even more on their guard and proceeded cautiously under the guidance of their scouts through a narrow path between sky-high mountains, where a large army could easily be destroyed with rolling stones. After this, they arrived in the small village of Maglan, where the peasants were well-armed but remained quiet. A certain Lord, living there in a castle, showed much politeness to Arnaud <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and military leader of the expedition.</note> and the other commanders, who found it necessary to take him and the village priest along as hostages. They also thought it best to proceed in some disorder from then on, so that their true number would not be accurately known. 

They now approached Salanche, the capital of the Duchy of Faucigny in Savoy, where they had to cross a famous bridge—at which a small band had held back a small army the year before—and where the Waldensians feared they would suffer a similar fate. Upon approaching, they could have won this important bridge through fighting with little effort; but as Christians, they wanted to avoid unnecessary bloodshed for as long as they could. Seeing [their condition], [Arnaud] desired that they should take breath and rest for a while in the abandoned huts of the Shepherds who inhabit these Mountains. While they made use of the huts, however, no one laid a hand on the property of the owners: the Hostages, surprised by such strictly observed military discipline <term>military discipline: <note>original: "krygstugt"</note> Refers to the rigorous code of conduct Arnaud enforced to distinguish his men from common bandits.</term>, received meager refreshment from this. They then urged the *Waldensians* to make use of the bread and cheese found there in the manner of war <note>In the "manner of war" implies foraging or taking necessary provisions during a campaign.</note>, and these men, also spurred by hunger, began to consume it; though not knowing to whom it belonged, they had to leave it unpaid. After a little rest, they judged it best to continue their way. All being encouraged again by their Commanders to climb the second Mountain with the same speed and unshaken courage, and to now double their alertness, a storm of snow and rain arose, so violent and thick that the Guide was terrified and completely at a loss; but encouraged by his followers, this treacherous Man regained his courage and led this small Army <note>original: "Krygsheir"</note> over this dangerous Mountain along the longest and most difficult path, in order meanwhile to give the *Savoyards* time to finish them off.

*Arnaud*, that zealous and diligent Leader of this small band of People, noticing this deceit of the Guide too late, found some Peasants along the way whom he took along as guides so as not to be misled any further; and furthermore, mingling himself among the ranks, he sought to lift the hearts of the fainting on this exhausting path through holy words of comfort and encouragement. On this second Mountain, they found passes and paths so narrow and steep to climb up and down as a ladder. Twenty Men could have destroyed an Army of 20,000 heads here.

### CHURCH HISTORY

If the ascent had been difficult for them, the descent was no less arduous, being accomplished for the most part by sitting and sliding, with no more light to guide them on this path than what the snow provided. All these hardships, however, like all things, were overcome through tireless persistence and patience. They finally arrived in a hamlet <term>hamlet: <note>original: "gehucht"</note> A small, isolated settlement, often consisting of just a few houses or huts.</term> inhabited by Shepherds, but situated so low that it felt as if they were descending and sinking into an abyss. The cold nipped at them fiercely, and desolation reigned there—and on top of that, it was so severe that they could find no fuel to warm themselves; nevertheless, they remained there that night to rest from the heavy journey.

#### IV. Day, a day of joy, after having suffered much discomfort.

The beginning of this day promised them little good. After some difficulties, the journey began, wading through snow up to their knees, while a falling rain soaked their bodies from above. Their path ran over rugged Mountains, where they found several fortifications <note>original: "verschanzingen"</note> which had been built previously out of fear that they might one day return by these places; but the fear of them having completely vanished, these works were entirely abandoned. This sight gladdened them so much that they sang a Hymn of Praise to God here in the open field, and before proceeding, solemnly thanked Him for this favorable providence <note>original: "bestelling"</note>. After this holy proceeding, they continued the journey, but the path became so narrow that no more than two could walk side by side. The Peasants, who could have crushed them all in this narrow pass with rolling stones, allowed them to pass through undisturbed; however, shortly thereafter, they rang the alarm bell, setting everything in an uproar and occupying the nearest Bridge that had to be crossed.

The Count of *Iseré*, a Gentleman of the Bedchamber to the Duchess, nevertheless found it advisable to grant the *Waldensians* passage and to restrain the Peasants: yet he, fearing—as had happened to others—that he would be taken along as a Hostage, fled away in great haste. The Army then moved forward and camped near the small town of *Sey* <note>modern-day Séez in the French Alps</note>, where they provided themselves with provisions <term>provisions: <note>original: "leeftogt"</note> Food and supplies necessary for a journey or military campaign.</term> and spent the fourth night.

### V. Day; a day of prosperity, followed by a good evening.

They undertook to continue their journey very early: several places were found abandoned: others were crowded with People who had come to see the passing *Waldensians*, about whom such a great rumor had spread: some *Savoyard* Lords urged them to take a day of rest there, to which they at first lent an ear and halted; but *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and military leader who led the "Glorious Return" of the Waldensians</note> arriving there with the rearguard, and distrusting the flattering invitations, made the Army march on through a dangerous Valley, whose Inhabitants had fled to the tops of the Mountains. Evening fell when they arrived in the Village of *Laval*, where they found an unusually good reception. The most prominent men of the Village offered fire and refreshments: *Arnaud* and his colleague *Montoux*, who in eight days had hardly eaten, drunk, or slept, here slept for three hours on a bed.

### VI. Day, a day of bad news.

On this day, they passed through the Village of *Tigne* <note>modern-day Tignes</note>, where previously, as recounted above (*), two *Waldensians* had been captured as Spies (as they had indeed been sent out with that intention, to gather information on how things stood with their Valleys and the roads <margin>(*) Page 85.</margin>

### VII. Day, a day of heavy toil.

Now they had a journey to undertake which *Hannibal*, the famous general of the *Carthaginians*, had made so many centuries before: that is, they had to climb Mount *Cenis*, the most famous of the *Alps*, because the road from *Savoy* to *Piedmont* runs over it. On the side of *Lanslebourg* <note>original: "Lasnebrug"; a village at the foot of the Mont Cenis pass</note> it is an hour high, dangerous and terrifying, because sometimes great snowdrifts, heavy blocks of ice, and violent stones tumble down from above. They nevertheless undertook this journey, and were hardly on their way when the mules belonging to Cardinal *Angelo Ranuzzi* <note>Ranuzzi (1626–1689) was a papal diplomat who had been serving as nuncio in Paris and was returning to Rome for the papal conclave.</note> traveling to *Rome*, fell into their hands, though they let them go. ->VIII. Day, a day of combat and victory.<-

They discovered in the morning light that armed peasants and *French* troops were positioned on the mountain peaks, and that the paths below were low and narrow; consequently, everything looked dangerous; nevertheless, they took heart. *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and military leader of the Waldensians during this expedition.</note> reinforced the vanguard with a hundred men upon whom the enemy, as soon as they were within reach, opened fire. *Arnaud*, seeing that little could be accomplished in the narrow passes, decided to seize the heights with his men. This order having been given, everyone crawled on hands and feet with indescribable effort up and down the precipices, which the *Hostages* <note>original: "Gyzelaars"; individuals from the local Catholic population taken by the Waldensians to ensure safe passage through hostile territory.</note> found so difficult that they prayed to be deprived of life. Some *Waldensians*, unable to follow the others as quickly and thus falling somewhat behind, were taken prisoner and afterward transported to *Turin*. Two of their commanders took the path through the woods, but nothing more was ever heard of them. This trek indeed cost them many people, but this loss did not rob them of their courage. They knew that God is accustomed to perform His wonders not through violence or the strength of arms, but by the humblest of means: rising higher with these thoughts, they discovered 200 armed soldiers on the mountains, whose commander sent word that they had nothing to fear from him if they marched past his post to the side. IX. Day, a day more pleasant than all previous days.

Now the courageous though exhausted *Waldensians* found themselves upon Mount *Sci*, where they halted to wait for those who had fallen behind. This was indeed a delightful place for the brave *Arnaud* and his followers: here he called all his people together and pointed with his finger to the peaks of the mountains they had formerly inhabited. He showed them their Fatherland <note>The Waldensian Valleys of Piedmont, their ancestral home from which they had been forcibly exiled three years earlier.</note> from afar, to their unspeakable joy. There, he exhorted them to praise God in that place, and offered such a powerful prayer that they stood up from their knees wonderfully strengthened and filled with joy. After they had solemnly thanked God, their mighty Helper, they undertook the final leg of their journey with cheers, and finally descended with indescribable joy and courage into the Valley of *Pragelas*, where they received their first refreshments and heard that the

[They set out] early, but the rain hindered the early march. The night and the rain overtook them to such an extent that they could not continue their march without burning torches, until they arrived at open barns where they did not sleep, but only dried themselves as best they could.

->XI. Day, a day of prosperity.<-

They rejoiced on this day at their arrival in the first village of the Valley of ***St. Martin***, where they rested and took 46 enemies prisoner, who were condemned to death in a council of war. <note>In the desperate circumstances of their return, the Waldensians often felt unable to take prisoners due to the risk of betrayal or slowing their pace.</note>

->XII. Day, a day of holy zeal and comfort.<-

Religious zeal prompted them on this day to burn down a Roman Catholic chapel, built after their expulsion from the Valleys. With joy, they saw that the Church of the Village of ***Guigou*** <note>Specifically the hamlet of Guigou in the parish of Prali.</note> was still standing; having torn out the Roman trappings and church ornaments, they sang together Psalm 74:

> *O God, why hast Thou cast us off for ever? Why doth Thine anger smoke against the sheep of Thy pasture? &c.*

***Arnaud*** then had Psalm 129 sung:

> *Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth up, &c.*

After these songs had been sung with the required reverence, ***Arnaud***, as Commander, laid aside his sword and, having donned his cloak as a Minister, climbed into the pulpit and delivered a soul-stirring sermon on several verses of the last song.

# CHURCH HISTORY

### XIII. Day.
After ***Arnaud*** <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and colonel who led the Waldensians back to their valleys.</note> had performed the public prayer as was his custom, they prepared to descend into the ***Luserna Valley*** <note>Now known as Val Pellice, a traditional stronghold of the Waldensian faith.</note>. Shortly thereafter, they captured one of the enemy’s scouts, who declared that he had been sent to spy on them, and that the Duke’s troops were well-entrenched not far from there. Upon hearing this, they divided themselves into three groups, seized a height from the boastful enemy, and pressed forward to attack them and their fortifications; just as they also, after a battle of half an hour, drove them out and captured all their baggage. Through this, they won ***Mount Julian***, though the rain halted their further progress.

### XIV. Day.
The beautiful morning urged the brave ***Waldensians*** to continue their march, but upon hearing of the flight of the enemies, they remained in the ***Village of Sibaud*** to rest.

### XV. Day.
After a skirmish with the enemies, they marched into the ***Town of Bobbio***, which had been abandoned by its inhabitants. They plundered the town, and another dispatched band brought back several prisoners.

### XVI. Day.
The excellent ***Montoux*** <note>Cyrille Montoux, a pastor and colleague of Arnaud during the expedition.</note>, an associate of ***Arnaud***, had the door of a house placed upon the tops of two rocks this day. Having climbed upon it, he delivered a sermon from this new pulpit—constructed without much forethought or ornament—on ***Luke 16:16***: <note>original: "De Wet en de Profeeten zyn tot op Joannes: van dien tyd af word het Koningryke Gods verkondigd, en een iegelyk doet geweld op het zelve."</note> *The law and the prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached, and every man presseth into it.* Following this, a great Assembly was held, and several laws were made, which were sworn with a solemn oath: <note>This event is known as the "Oath of Sibaud," where the Waldensians swore mutual loyalty and religious discipline.</note>

### XVII. Day.

After the Prayer was performed, they set out to attack *Villars* <note>Villar Pellice, a key town in the Waldensian valleys.</note>. The enemies abandoned the Town and retreated into the Monastery, from which they directed a terrible fire upon their attackers. *Arnaud*, having devised a stratagem, had several barrels brought into the streets, behind which some of his *Waldensians* hid themselves against the flying bullets, while others broke into the houses situated closest to the Monastery, from which they fired upon the enemy. The prisoners said that the besieged had little provisions, and this moved *Arnaud* to spare his people and starve the enemy out. They intercepted 14 mules, laden with provisions, sent to the besieged; the enemies, making a sortie upon this, were repulsed by the brave *Waldensians*, and the enemy Commander, the *Baron de Choüate* <note>An officer in the service of the Duke of Savoy.</note>, lost his life there.

### XVIII. Day.

The enemies abandoned the Monastery on this day: many of them fell by the hands of the pursuing *Waldensians*. The Duke’s troops now increased so greatly in number that the *Waldensians*, fearing they would be cut off from one another, left *Villars* in some unavoidable disorder. They were somewhat scattered during that retreat. Eighty men were miraculously preserved and arrived safely on the mountain of *Vendelin* <note>Col Vandalin, a high ridge overlooking the valley.</note>. ### XIX. Day.

On which a reinforcement was sent to *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor-colonel leading the expedition.</note>, in order to capture the mountains of *Angrogne*.

### XX. Day.

*Arnaud* sought to make some discoveries <note>Reconnaissance or scouting missions.</note> on this day, on which occasion, accompanied only by six *Waldensians*, he took some laden mules as booty.

### XXI. Day.

A woman, who after their expulsion from the Valleys had been forced into apostasy <term>afval; the forced conversion from the Waldensian/Reformed faith to Catholicism during the years of exile</term>, brought *Arnaud* some refreshments and begged him to spare the life of her husband, a *Savoyard* <note>A subject of the Duke of Savoy, the sovereign who had originally expelled the Waldensians.</note>, which was granted to her. On that day, some provisions and prisoners were obtained, and *Arnaud* received a reinforcement of 200 men, who had been separated from him since the 18th day. He performed a public and solemn thanksgiving to God for the advantages gained, and thereafter defeated several small bands of the enemy.

### XXII. Day.

Which was mainly spent seeking provisions.

### XXIII. and XXIV. Day.

*Arnaud* administered the Holy Supper <term>Avondmaal; the sacrament of Communion or the Eucharist</term> for the first time in the Valleys, cared for the wounded, and obtained some booty.

### XXV. Day.

The enemies burned down several villages; the rain prevented the *Waldensians* from paying them back for this.

### XXVI. Day.
News was received that *French* troops were coming to assist the Duke of *Savoy*, whereupon some scouts were dispatched.

### XXVII. Day.
On which the scouts returned and brought news that 8,000 *Frenchmen* had arrived at the bridge of *Salabertran* <note>Salbertrand; the site of a major battle earlier in their expedition where the Waldensians defeated a much larger French force to secure their passage.</note>; however, upon the rumor that the *Spaniards* had besieged *Casal* <note>Casale Monferrato, a strategically important fortified city in the Piedmont region.</note>, they departed.

### XXVIII. Day.
After Prayer, some were sent out to make discoveries <note>Reconnaissance or scouting missions to determine enemy positions.</note>.

### XXIX. Day.
They engaged in hand-to-hand combat with a band of 500 Enemies; a thunderstorm with rain caused them to retreat with losses.

### XXX. Day.
They allowed the Inhabitants of the Valley of *Pragelas* <note>The Val Pragelato, a high mountain valley that was a frequent site of conflict between French and Savoyard interests.</note> to gather their grape harvest, provided that they would provide a certain sum of money. They took some wine as booty, and drank together to the health of *William III*, *King of Great Britain*, the *States General of the United Netherlands*, the *Elector of Brandenburg*, and the *Duke of Schomberg* <note>A list of the primary Protestant allies of the Waldensians. Frederick Schomberg was a famous Huguenot general who served William III.</note>. Furthermore, several enemy bands were driven off 그날, and two men were hanged who had served the *Marquis of Parelle* as Spies.

### XXXI. Day.
Thus on this day the *Waldensians* became complete masters of the Valley of *St. Martin* <note>Valle di San Martino, one of the three historic Waldensian Valleys.</note>; with which we close this Journal, believing this to be sufficient to give the Reader an idea of this famous expedition through almost inaccessible places, bravely undertaken and successfully carried out by a handful of *Waldensians*.

### CHAPTER XII.

*An Interlude, in which a report is given on how things fared with the Waldensians who stayed behind.*

We have stated above (*) that Arnaud, with his 800 or 900 *Waldensians* <note>The Waldensians were a pre-Reformation Christian movement from the Alpine valleys, often persecuted for their beliefs.</note>, did not cross the *Lake of Geneva* at the appointed time and place except after he had waited in vain for some who arrived too late, and for whose sake he could not place the main body in extreme danger by continuing to wait. These people, arriving too late at the meeting place and finding *Arnaud* gone, decided to follow. Some, who previously did not want to march without weapons and considered the others reckless, now also took this into their heads; but in particular, some common folk appeared who, accustomed to marveling at news of novelties, gathered together upon reports of *Arnaud’s* success and determined (as they carried out on the 11th of September <note>original: "Herffstmaand," a traditional Dutch name for September, literally "Harvest Month."</note>) under the leadership of *Bourgeois*, a brave Commander, to first sail across the *Lake of Geneva*, and thereafter follow in the footsteps of the others. 

They comprised together 13 bands of *French Refugees* <note>These were likely Huguenots, French Protestants who had fled to Switzerland after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685.</note>, 3 bands of *Swiss*, and 2 of *Waldensians*. As soon as they had crossed the Lake into *Savoy*, they indeed defeated some resisting Countryfolk, yet for lack of good guides, they made little progress; and many at the same time gave themselves over to robbery and looting; but soon suffering a lack of provisions, they became so divided that *Bourgeois*, no longer being able to keep his bands in good order—

Thus poorly did this undertaking turn out. It was no true zeal to restore Religion in the Valleys of *Piedmont* that had urged the irregular bands of *Bourgeois* (who deserved a better fate) to this enterprise; rather, driven mostly by a thirst for glory and jealousy over *Arnaud’s* brave deeds, they wished to follow him in their own manner and share in the glory, which then brought such unfortunate consequences in its wake. Thus, the outcomes often correspond so little to the initial expectations one had formed of them.

The King of *France* and the Duke of *Savoy* had now heard with great astonishment and even greater displeasure not only of the return of the *Waldensians* to their Valleys, but also of their glorious deeds which they performed there; *France* thereupon decided to send an army for their extermination, and the Duke of *Savoy*, due to his alliance with that King, saw himself forced to employ another of 12,000 men; to which the Duke probably would not have easily decided, as the sequel shall teach us, if *France* had not pressured him into it. These armies, spurred on by strict orders, now descended without delay toward the Valleys.

*The Waldensians*, hearing this, considered all lost unless God turned away this threatening storm. *They*, trusting in Him, nevertheless decided not to surrender without a blow, much less to abandon in an instant their Fatherland, won so dearly <note>Literally "so sourly," meaning with great hardship and bitterness.</note> with the sword; but if they absolutely had to die, they would much rather perish in the same for the cause of God.

*Arnaud* then first gathered all his bands, which had been scattered since the 3rd of September <note>Dutch: *Herfstmaand*, the "harvest month."</note>; this was not easily accomplished, because many had to fight their way through the enemies before they could reunite with their brothers. This frank language from their beloved Teacher and Commander <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), who served both as a pastor and the military leader of the Waldensians during their "Glorious Return."</note>, spoken with great earnestness, struck them; he saw it, and without waiting for an answer, he knelt down and most fervently prayed to God for wisdom and strength in these most perilous circumstances. Rising from his knees, he delivered an oration, and therein brought to their attention: "what a great undertaking they had carried out thus far through the hand of God; — what a dangerous journey they had overcome; — how, with sword in hand, they had traversed *Savoy* and had now taken their Valleys; — that the honor for this belonged to God, whose love for the restoration of the uprooted Gospel in the Valleys had so visibly blessed and approved their courage, zeal, and unity in achieving this momentous task, so that the whole world would stand amazed at this work of the Lord when it heard that they had already entirely mastered a Valley in such a short time; — that if ever unity were needed, it was now; — that to separate from one another was nothing other than to walk toward certain death; furthermore, that one did not know how God, who was mighty to deliver them from the greatest needs and had already shown this so often, might be able to rescue them from the hands of two powerful armies; — in a word, that there was now no other course to choose than to take refuge at *Balsille* (*)." etc.

What influence does a courageous General, who is at the same time an eloquent Teacher <note>Arnaud was a pastor as well as a military commander; his "teaching" refers to his sermons and spiritual guidance.</note>, not have on the hearts of pious bands such as these? They had nothing to bring against *Arnaud’s* reasons but agreed with them entirely and promised to follow him wherever he should lead them. With joy, *Arnaud* saw heroism and unity revive in his despondent troops, and no other difficulty remained for him than this one, which was indeed great enough: namely, how he would bring his *Waldensians* to *Balfille* <note>La Balsille, a steep, rocky peak in the San Martino Valley that served as a natural fortress.</note>. To this end, a fortunate stratagem occurred to the ever-contemplating General. He decided to deceive the enemy by having his people raise fortifications during the day and feign an intention to defend themselves there to the last man. He undertook and carried out this work but, as evening fell, suddenly ceased it, urged his people to prepare for the march, and made a skillful yet difficult and dangerous retreat by night over such mountains and rugged rocks that they often had to crawl across them on hands and feet; so that, had they seen the path they had clambered over during the day, their hair would have stood on end—just as they later remembered their perilous journey with astonishment and horror when they beheld those rocks they had crossed.

Safely they arrived at *Balfille*, and decided no longer to let themselves be hunted over the mountains like partridges <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 26:20, comparing their persecution to a hunt for wild birds.</note>, climbing rocks up and down and exhausting themselves completely, but to choose the most advantageous post here and fortify themselves within it as strongly as possible.

...unsuccessful attack <note>The word "unsuccessful" (Dutch: *ongelukkig*) is split between the previous page and this one.</note>, further away. *Arnaud*, who the previous day had conducted himself as a brave and capable warrior, behaved today as befits a true Minister <note>The original Dutch uses *Leeraar* (Teacher), a common term for a Protestant minister or pastor at the time.</note>. They obeyed this word so cheerfully and readily that he had barely finished his sermon before each man brought the captured plunder before him, which he accurately divided, leaving some surplus to be distributed among the poor. Furthermore, he took care of a captured French Commander with such nobility that even his enemies praised him for it.

Thus vainly did this plan of the enemies come to an end—among whom were some who had already firmly concluded that all *Waldensians* would be put to death within six hours. Others, however, feared that they would not be so easily driven from that advantageous position and that much blood would be shed on both sides beforehand. The outcome deceived them in everything, as has been heard.

The enemy armies had not withdrawn to abandon all further undertakings entirely, but only to devise better measures for the destruction of the *Waldensians*. Experience had taught the enemies that their opposing party, thus entrenched, was invincible and all similar attacks were powerless. The proposal was, despite the danger, generally accepted, and they made themselves ready for travel in the evening, while the enemy continued shooting. *Poulat* made them take off their shoes at midnight, so as not to make any noise on the rocks, but to get away in silence. He was the first, and they all followed him: the plan, however difficult in execution over such rocks, succeeded, and the enemies did not discover until late in the day that they had all escaped the trap <note>The Dutch idiom *den dans ontsprongen* literally means "escaped the dance," signifying a narrow escape from a dangerous situation.</note>. They hoped, wished, and prayed that the latter might happen, and then considered the loss of *Balsille* <note>The mountain fortress the Waldensians had just been forced to abandon.</note>—indeed, all their losses—to be richly compensated.

The reader may perhaps wonder why this news was so welcome to the *Waldensians*. To unravel this, we must necessarily give him an idea of Europe’s situation at that time, in which the *Waldensians* had the greatest interest. *William III*, King of *England*, along with the *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> and the *Emperor*, had declared war on *France* in the year 1689; the *Emperor*, together with *Spain*, then invited the Duke of *Savoy* to break his alliance with *France* and cross over to their side. *Victor Amadeus II* <note>The Duke of Savoy, whose territory included the Waldensian valleys; he had previously been a fierce persecutor of the group under French pressure.</note> foresaw, on the one hand, that En—

Such harsh and unacceptable conditions were dictated to him by *France*, in the hope that they would force the Duke to remain in his old alliances with them. But the Duke, being master neither of himself nor of his states at that time, demanded time for deliberation, and in the meantime wrote to the aforementioned *Allied Princes* <note>The powers of the Grand Alliance, formed to oppose the expansionism of Louis XIV.</note> to ask if they would assist him against *France* if he chose their side. They promised it, and *Spain* immediately thereafter declared war on *France*.

The Duke, long provoked by the pride with which *France* had treated him, now heard that its King <note>Louis XIV of France.</note> was currently offering the *Waldensians* full restoration to their old possessions and free exercise of religion in their *Valleys*, on the condition that they allied themselves with him. He decided to forestall *France*, making use of the assistance of *England* and *Holland* promised to the *Waldensians*, and not wanting to let his *Valleys* be lost into the hands of *France*; therefore, he judged it best to make peace with the *Waldensians* as quickly as possible.

Wondrous arrangement of *God's Providence*! That King, who had been the primary cause of their miserable expulsion from their *Fatherland*, now provides the first occasion for their restor-

When *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor-colonel who led the Waldensian "Glorious Return."</note> and his men, on the 18th of May <note>original: "Bloeimaand," the month of blossoms.</note>, after having taken the village of *Rúa*, climbed the Mountains of *Angrogne* to go out for plunder, he was not a little surprised that two envoys of Baron *Pallavicini*, in the name of the Duke of *Savoy*, came to offer him peace and all necessary provisions, of which they were in great need. Having marched not much further, the Knight of *Vercellis* let them know that he would gladly hold a conference with their commanders. In the meantime, they lacked all kinds of provisions. One of *Arnaud's* companies here shot a partridge and offered it to him, but he, having had it roasted, gave it to four hungry prisoners, saying: "Today we eat partridges without bread; the time will come when we shall eat bread without partridges." Finally, by order of the Duke, all kinds of supplies were sent to them, and they received with unspeakable joy these first signs of full peace. Also, Baron *Pallavicini* immediately informed the Duke's troops, and particularly the Governor of *Mirebouc*, that peace with the *Waldensians* had been concluded, and that he must allow them to go freely and frankly wherever they wished. Furthermore, he invited the *French* Refugees to come find a safe shelter in the Valleys, as is evident from this document below (*).

### CHAPTER XIV.

*The Waldensians having united with their Duke, turn their weapons against France for six years, that is, from 1690 to 1697.*

Arnaud <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor-colonel who led the Waldensian "Glorious Return."</note>, now regarded as a subject of the Duke and General of the *Waldensians*, received word on his behalf that war against *France* had been declared; at the same time, he was ordered to occupy *Villars* and *Bobi* <note>Villar Pellice and Bobbio Pellice, key villages in the Waldensian Valleys.</note>, which had been abandoned by the Duke's army, with his own men, to make use of the provisions stored there in the warehouses, and henceforth to turn his weapons against the *French*. *Arnaud* then marched there, and shortly after his arrival he was surprised by some of his friends, among whom were the two captains *Palene* and *Mondon*, who, along with others, had been released and set free from their prison in *Turin* by order of the Duke. The release of all prisoners and the arrival of these men caused general joy among the *Waldensians*: they heard from the mouths of these gentlemen the obliging words of the Duke, who had said, "I do not wish to prevent you from preaching the Gospel anywhere, not even in *Turin* itself," etc.

Baron *Palavicini*, commanding the Duke's troops, intending to seek out the *French*—who had retreated into the *Queyras* Valley <note>A valley in the French High Alps, bordering the Waldensian territory.</note> after the declaration of war—ordered the *Waldensians* to attack them from one side while he would engage them from the other. Grateful for the peace they had received, and wishing to prove their unshakable loyalty to their generous Duke, they sent out 300 men for this undertaking. After prayer was led by *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud, the pastor-commander of the Waldensians.</note>, they launched an attack on a *French* village, which they captured, burned, and plundered. Laden with much booty, they returned to *Bobbio* <note>Bobbio Pellice, one of the primary Waldensian strongholds.</note>, where the spoils were divided, and some of the seized goods were sent to the Duke as a gift. The Knight of *Vercelli* came here to meet *Arnaud*, eager to see the brave *Waldensians*, and they afterwards went to speak with Baron *Palavicini* to make some plans regarding general affairs.

Several persons from the parish of *Torre Pellice* <note>The cultural and religious center of the Waldensian Valleys.</note>, who in the previous persecution had succumbed to the force of temptation and had abandoned the pure religion <note>A term used by the Waldensians to describe their reformed faith, which they believed remained untainted by Roman Catholic additions.</note>, now returned. Weighted with shame and repentance, they prayed to be readmitted into the bosom of the Church. The number of *Waldensians* increased from day to day through these individuals and other released prisoners, among whom were *Montoux* and *Chyon*, *Arnaud's* colleagues.

One of *Arnaud's* captains, sent out for plunder, had the good fortune to intercept a *French* courier carrying a valise of letters of the utmost importance, dispatched to the *French* army. He brought him safely to *Arnaud* in *Bobbio*. *Arnaud* brought him to Baron *Palavicini*, who subsequently sent *Arnaud* along with the courier to the Duke.

This was an excellent compensation both for the bitter scorn that had been shown to this worthy Man during his expulsion, and for the misery he had suffered to restore the Gospel of the great Redeemer in the Valleys, in which he had so wondrously succeeded through Divine Providence.

Amazing reversal of affairs! This *Arnaud*, for whom the Roman Catholic *Swiss*—at the time of his wanderings in the *Protestant Cantons*—had so often lain in wait to capture him, to bring him then to *Constance*, and to deal with him just as they had done there with *Jan Hus* and *Jerome of Prague* at the stake in the year 1416 <note>Hus and Jerome were early reformers burned for heresy by the Council of Constance; the author draws a parallel to the danger Arnaud faced.</note>: this *Arnaud*, I say, now saw himself delivered from the hands of his haters and in deep favor with his Prince. He, who was no richer than 10 *pistoles* <term>A gold coin used across Europe, typically of Spanish or French origin.</term> when he undertook the great expedition from *Switzerland* through *Savoy*, and had only half a *louis* <term>A French gold coin, the Louis d'or.</term> remaining when he arrived in the Valleys, now received Princely gifts. He, who four years ago saw the light of the Gospel extinguished here, now saw and helped to rekindle it anew, and obtained all the old privileges and freedoms for the *Waldensians* once again.

King *William III* <note>The Dutch Prince of Orange who became King of England, Scotland, and Ireland in 1689.</note> and the *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, having heard that he and his *Waldensians* had forced their way through *Savoy* into *Piedmont* with sword in hand, had given them all up for lost; but learning of their brave deeds, they sent him more support, and had

# ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

At this time, some *French Refugees* from *Switzerland* and *Brandenburg* came down to their aid. *William* <note>King William III of England and Prince of Orange, a key protector of Protestant interests in Europe.</note> afterward raised him to the rank of *Colonel* over the bands that he paid, and for that purpose sent him an *Act* <term>A formal legal document or commission of appointment.</term> to that end. (*)

The *Waldensians*, now restored to their old possessions, served their Duke this year with all bravery and loyalty; indeed, if they, together with *King William III* and the *Dutch*, had not powerfully assisted him against *France*, he would have suddenly fallen prey to the *French*: since the *Emperor* and *Spain* failed to send him the promised aid. The *Emperor* did, however, send General *Caraffa* to him the following year, 1691, with an army, but he accomplished little as he thwarted many good proposals. *Montmélian* <note>A strategic fortress in the Duchy of Savoy.</note> was lost through his fault. *King William III* then sent over the young Duke of *Schomberg* <note>Charles de Schomberg, a Huguenot general who served in the Williamite forces.</note> to take command of the troops which the King paid; and the *Waldensians*, although they could not live peacefully in their *Valleys* because they had to serve the Duke in the field, nevertheless received much good in these circumstances through *William's* power and generosity.

*Schomberg*, who could rely on the *Waldensians* and was certain that many *Reformed* <note>Referring to the Huguenots, French Protestants who had fled religious persecution in France.</note> from *Dauphiné* would join him, undertook to relieve *Montmélian*, which was besieged by the *French*: but *Caraffa* and the *Court of Turin* seemed more afraid (†) of the strength of Heresy <note>The Catholic court feared the growing influence of the Protestant (heretical) forces more than their French enemies.</note> than of the power of *France*; and preferred to let that important place fall into their hands rather than have it relieved by him. In the year 1692, at the opening of the campaign, the *Waldensians*—who had now spent a winter peacefully in their Valleys and enjoyed the free exercise of their religion—took to the field with the Duke. He led his army into *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>, and he had no cause to complain that the *Waldensians* had abandoned their ancient courage. Had he pursued matters with the same fire with which he began, he would have thrown the *French* on that side into even greater disorder. He laid siege to *Embrun* <note>original: "Ambrun"</note>; this city would have been captured by him at the very start had there not been great weakness or much treachery among his advisors, but as it was, the siege cost him several weeks. When smallpox <term>A highly contagious and often fatal viral disease; in the 17th century, it frequently decided the fate of military campaigns.</term> subsequently afflicted him and put his life in danger, he was forced to retreat. The *Waldensians* prayed to God for the extension of his life, and they were heard.

In the year 1693, the campaign was opened late: it was not until July <note>original: "Hooymand", literally 'Hay-month'.</note> that the Duke marched against the *French* with his army, in which the *Waldensians* were once again included, forcing their General *Catinat* <note>Nicolas Catinat, a Marshal of France.</note> to retreat. He then besieged *Santa Brigida* <note>original: "Bridget", a strategic fort near Pinerolo.</note>, a fort above *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, and became master of it after twelve days. Not being well-provided with artillery, however, he had to abandon the siege of *Pinerolo*. At the end of that campaign, *Catinat*, having reinforced his army, marched against the Duke of *Savoy*; they came to blows at *Orbassano* <note>The Battle of Marsaglia, fought on October 4, 1693.</note>. The *Waldensians* fought with all heroism under the very eyes of the Duke. The *French* claimed the honor of the fight, but at the same time suffered the greatest losses: for the Duke won that day

In the year 1694, the Duke took into mature consideration the significant services rendered to him by *Arnaud* <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), a pastor and military leader who famously led the Waldensians back to their ancestral valleys in the "Glorious Return."</note> and the *Waldensians* in the previous campaigns. On the 23rd of May <note>original: "Bloeymaand", literally 'Blossom-month', an archaic Dutch term for May.</note>, at the request of *King William III* and the *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, he decided by a new Edict to solemnly restore them forever to all their ancient privileges. Indeed, one is obliged to give honor to the Dukes of *Savoy* for having confirmed and observed this Edict at all times; for this reason, one must also attribute the fact that their thirteen churches have remained standing to this day to that very decree. Touched by this royal generosity, they took to the field with him in joy.

The English then appeared with their fleet before Toulon; because of this, the French were forced to keep their troops at home to protect their coast and were prevented from coming to the aid of Casale <note>A strategic fortress in the Piedmont region</note>, as a result of which the city was finally won.

The following year, 1696, brought much displeasure to the *Waldensians*. The Pope and the *Venetians* intended to have the *Germans* <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Empire's forces</note> move out of *Italy*, to release the Duke of *Savoy* from the war, and to make him no longer dependent on *England* and *Holland*, whose King and States they called heretics. ### CHAPTER XV.

*All French Refugees, including Mr. Arnaud <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the famous pastor and military leader who led the Waldensians in their "Glorious Return" to their valleys.</note>, being pressured by France, are forced to leave the Valleys and depart for Germany; together with the painful consequences of that departure for the Waldensians, from 1697 to 1699.*

The year 1697 is famous in history for the Peace concluded at Ryswick <note>The Treaty of Ryswick ended the Nine Years' War between France and the Grand Alliance (England, Spain, and the Holy Roman Empire).</note> between the principal Sovereigns of Europe. To everyone's misfortune, no advantages for the Protestants in the Palatinate <note>A region in southwestern Germany that had been devastated during the war.</note> and France were stipulated in its Articles. The French Refugees, hearing this, therefore applied to King William III <note>William of Orange, King of England and Stadtholder of the Netherlands.</note> and the other Protestant Allies, praying that they would think of them; but since they had had no part in the cause of the War, William could do nothing else but most emphatically recommend them to France. Yet its King <note>Louis XIV, known as the "Sun King."</note> was so given over to superstition and cruelty that their condition became even worse after the Peace than before; for the Court now had more time to keep an eye on them and to persecute them more sharply than it had judged advisable during the War. The Valleys received the first consequences of this in the following year, 1698.

The King of France, resentful toward so many inhabitants who, after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes <note>The 1685 decree by Louis XIV that abolished the rights of French Protestants (Huguenots), leading to mass emigration.</note>, had fled the Kingdom for their religion and had found shelter with the Duke of Savoy—indeed, who had entered his service against him during the last War—now allowed himself to be so carried away by revenge and a desire for persecution that he pressured the Duke of Savoy so long,

The Illustrious Duke of *Württemberg*, *Eberhard* <note>Eberhard Louis, Duke of Württemberg (1676–1733), who provided refuge to the Waldensians and Huguenots.</note>, honored *Arnaud*—who was settling within his territory—with an estate, which we are accustomed to calling a lordship <term>Heerlykheid: a manorial estate or territory over which a lord held specific legal and financial rights</term>. After he had settled here, he requested in the year 1700 of King *William* III <note>William of Orange, King of England, who was a staunch defender of the Protestant cause in Europe.</note> to be allowed to share in the 400 pounds sterling which had been designated by the late Queen *Mary* for the maintenance of the Ministers of the *Piedmontese* Valleys. For even though they were French by birth and now living abroad, he believed he was justified in making this request, as they had for a long time performed service in the Valleys as Ministers of the *Waldensians*.

The esteem which *William* III held for *Arnaud*—on account of his excellent zeal, illustrious deeds, and great services rendered to the Valleys—resulted in the King not only granting 140 pounds sterling for the Ministers of those seven mentioned churches in *Germany* but also endowing him with a special pension, both as a reward for his brave deeds and to enable him to live with his family in honor and prestige. Here, with his newly established congregation, *Arnaud* enjoyed not only a pleasant rest after so many calamities but also the pleasure of seeing the prosperity of his flock, and

This royal word <note>This refers to a promise made by the Duke of Savoy, Victor Amadeus II, who was often referred with royal titles due to his sovereign status.</note> reassured them well, but it was not capable of making up for the painful loss of seven Ministers <note>original: "Leeraaren," literally "teachers," but used historically to refer to ordained clergy or pastors.</note>. The few who remained and were now their only comfort found themselves unable to properly look after the thirteen communities of the Valleys, especially during the winter time. If ever, the Ministers were now most necessary to them, to preach the good word of God and train in sound doctrine the *Waldensians* who had wandered everywhere and now returned, but who lacked instruction and edification in this time of pleasant rest and safety.

The *Swiss*, their old friends and fellow believers, helped them in this extremely great predicament. The illustrious Canton of Bern and the noble government of Geneva, who had so often assisted them, decided to request the Duke to allow seven other Ministers to be sent to the Valleys immediately in place of those who had departed; this was granted to them, and thereupon seven were chosen and sent off. They received these with joy and recognized the excellent favor the *Swiss* showed them in this: but their joy would have been even greater had they known how to support these Ministers and reward their labor as it deserved. Their Synod <term>Synod: a formal council of church leaders gathered to manage the affairs and doctrines of their churches</term>, held on the 1st of August <note>original: "Oogstmaand," the traditional Dutch name for August, the harvest month.</note> in the year 1699 at *Angrogne*, drew up a detailed report on this matter, of which I currently have a copy before me, and sent it to the Honorable Church Council of Geneva; complaining therein: that, since 13 Ministers, and as many schoolmasters, besides a *Rector* <term>Rector: in this context, the headmaster or lead teacher of a grammar school</term>, who instructed the youth in the *Latin* language—

The failing health of the King of *Spain* <note>Charles II, the last Habsburg ruler of Spain, whose death without an heir triggered a major European crisis.</note> at the end of this year alarmed *Europe*, since, should he die without heirs, a new war threatened to break out in which the *Waldensians* would also be entangled. *France*, the *Emperor*, and *Bavaria* all had designs on that Crown. The Duke of *Savoy* <note>Victor Amadeus II, whose territories were strategically located between France and the Habsburg lands in Italy.</note> might also possibly obtain it, if he were willing to cede his states to *France*; however, *England* and *Holland* were not indifferent as to who acquired it. *William III*, being at *Het Loo* in *Gelderland* <note>A royal palace in the Netherlands used by William III as a summer residence and for diplomatic meetings.</note> at that time, worked with the *States-General* <note>original: "Algemeene Staaten," the governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> to quell the dispute in time and to help elect a Prince as successor to that Kingdom who could maintain the balance of *Europe*, which *France* wished to see tip to its own side. To this end, in the year 1700, the notorious *Partition Treaty* <note>The Second Partition Treaty, an attempt by European powers to divide the Spanish inheritance to prevent a general war.</note> was introduced to the world; the King of *Spain* subsequently died, and the Duke of *Anjou* succeeded him by Will. The *Emperor*, dissatisfied with this, sent Prince *Eugene* with an army to *Italy* against the *Frenchmen*, commanded by the Duke of *Savoy*, who, through the marriage of his second daughter to King *Philip*, was aligned with the interests of *France*; which interests he nevertheless pursued only half-heartedly in the year 1701. After King *William III* died in the year 1702 and *Anne* ascended the English Throne, and had declared war on *France* in 1703 alongside *Holland*, he chose—to preserve his own States—the side of *England* and *Holland*, who paid him 20,000 pounds sterling a month to wage the war.
The *Waldensians* had no reason to grieve over this turn of events and the choice of the Duke; they enjoyed peace under his rule and hoped to receive further benefits from this alliance.

To his misfortune, the Duke did not have enough troops to defend himself against the *French*; on the other hand, he managed his affairs with great prudence and showed more steadfastness in his misfortunes than one could have imagined. Prince *Eugene* <note>Prince Eugene of Savoy (1663–1736), a celebrated field marshal of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, sent by the Emperor to the Duke's aid, was having a difficult time in *Italy* then. He had a small Army of 8,000 Infantry and 4,000 Cavalry, and scarcely enough Land left to sustain them. *Turin* and *Cuneo* <note>original: "Coni"</note> were the only significant Places he still possessed; but he seemed to have resolved to be driven out of everything rather than abandon his Allies.

After several skirmishes had greatly reduced his forces, the Duke of *Feuillade* <note>Louis d'Aubusson, Duke of La Feuillade (1673–1725), the French general leading the siege of Turin.</note>, who directed the siege, drove him away from *Turin*. While the Place underwent a famous Siege, the *Waldensians* did not sit idle. Some of them had taken up positions in the Mountains of *Turin* to harass the *French*, while others lay in wait in the *Perouse* Valley <note>The Val Perosa, one of the three traditional Waldensian valleys in the Piedmont region.</note> to intercept the *Convoys* coming from *France* and going toward *Turin*, as they succeeded in doing several times. Yet however cautiously they might conduct themselves in this, they could not prevent the *Waldensians* from taking a good portion as booty.

Finally, Prince *Eugene* appeared from *Germany*, at a time when *Turin* found itself so greatly distressed that almost all the gunpowder was nearly spent and the place could not hold out the siege for two days longer. The Duke, hearing of his arrival, marched up from the Valleys, gathered his *Waldensians* and other bands together, and joined Prince *Eugene*. ### OF THE WALDENSIANS.

After various skirmishes had been greatly reduced, the Duke of *Feuillade* <note>Louis d'Aubusson, Duke of La Feuillade (1673–1725), the French general leading the siege.</note>, who directed the siege, drove him away from *Turin*. On this occasion, the *Waldensians* earned the glory of having covered their Prince’s retreat and secured him from the pursuit of his chasing enemies.

He took refuge in the Valleys of his faithful *Waldensians*, where he was safe, and waited there for the arrival of *Prince Eugene* <note>Prince Eugene of Savoy, a celebrated field marshal of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> to relieve *Turin*. While the place underwent a famous siege, the *Waldensians* did not sit idle. Some of them had taken positions on the Mountains of *Turin* to harass the *French*, while others lay in wait in the *Perouse* Valley <note>The Val Perosa, one of the three traditional Waldensian valleys in Piedmont.</note> to intercept the <term>convoys<gloss>Original: "Convoyen." These were guarded supply trains carrying food and ammunition.</gloss></term> coming from *France* and going toward *Turin*, in which they succeeded several times.

One of their small bands, having precise knowledge of all the mountain paths—which were very winding and involved many detours—had positioned itself so well that the *French* could receive no provisions or war equipment from *France* without taking great precautions. This hindered them tremendously in the siege; yet however cautiously they might behave, they could not prevent the *Waldensians* from taking a good portion as booty.

Finally, *Prince Eugene* appeared from *Germany*, when *Turin* found itself so distressed that nearly all the gunpowder had been spent and the place could not hold out against the siege for two days longer. The Duke, hearing of his arrival, marched out from the Valleys, gathered his *Waldensians* and other bands together, and joined *Prince Eugene*. Together they hurried toward that shattered and desperate place; they were 28,000 men strong, while the *French* numbered more than 40,000, entrenched in a fortified camp. Notwith-

Notwithstanding this unequal strength, the Duke <note>Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy (1666–1732).</note> attacked them, and after a resistance of two hours, he broke through, making such a violent slaughter that the *French* fled in the greatest disorder, divided into various bands, so that not even 1,600 remained united as they reached *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France bordering the Alps.</note>.

The *Waldensians* behaved in this battle no differently than before: they gathered much booty and then moved, under the guidance of the Duke and Prince *Eugene*, toward the *Milanese* territory. The City of *Milan* opened its gates to them; the *Citadel* <term>inner fortress<gloss>The central stronghold of a city, usually the last line of defense.</gloss></term> and other strong places offered resistance, but were taken after a short siege. Thus the campaign ended gloriously for the *Waldensians*: they saw their Duke rescued from distress and themselves set at liberty. They returned with joy and victory to their Valleys, and the Winter gave them rest.

At the beginning of the year 1707, the Duke made a plan to march his army into *France*, for which the *Waldensians* were ready. *France* meanwhile made proposals to him for *Peace*, and offered compensation for the destruction of his land under certain conditions that did not suit the Duke. He then marched on, pretending that he intended to invade *Dauphiné*, luring the *French* there; he then turned aside, marched toward *Toulon*, and bombarded the city. However, seeing the entire *French* power approaching him, he broke camp, returned without any loss, besieged *Susa* (*), and took the city with the help of the *Waldensians*.
