In the following year, 1708, the Duke <note>Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy.</note> took the small town of *Exilles* and *Fenestrella*, a fortress on the River *Cluson* <note>The Chisone River in the Piedmont region of Italy.</note>, and likewise the Valley of *St. Martin* <note>Val di San Martino, one of the three traditional Waldensian valleys.</note>, which was currently mostly abandoned by its inhabitants, who had already fled to the Valley of *Lucern* <note>Val Pellice.</note> three years earlier. It was evident from this that they had succumbed in their loyalty due to the overwhelming power of *France*; for which reason they were restored to full honor, and their previous disgrace was completely wiped out. They submitted themselves entirely to the Duke's obedience and obtained full pardon through the mediation of the Marquis of *Andorno*. Late in the summer, the Duke opened the campaign in *Savoy*: the *Waldensians* accompanied him once again on this expedition; he mastered everything that came before him and brought dismay everywhere, even as far as *Lyons*. He also took the Valley of *Pragelas* <note>Pragelato.</note>, by which an open road was cleared for him to make greater progress in the following campaign.

Had the Emperor <note>Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor.</note> been willing to satisfy the demands of the Duke of *Savoy* in this year of 1709, he would have penetrated deep into *France*; but since the Emperor had no desire for this, the Duke did not take the field in person, but let his troops fight only in a defensive manner: as a result, the *Waldensians* enjoyed more rest this year than before, and little blood was shed.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

*An unpleasant scene opened in the Valley of Pragelas in the following year, 1730, when the Reformed religion was completely eradicated there.*

Up to this point, we have described the fortunes of the three Valleys <note>Referring to the valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, and San Martino.</note>, properly called the Valleys of Piedmont, in succession as briefly as possible, and have said little of a fourth called Pragelas, in order to treat it more extensively in this appropriate place. In ancient times, this fourth Valley stood, like the other three, under the domain of the Dukes of Savoy and Princes of Piedmont, who afterwards lost it through France's superior power and arms. For nearly two centuries it remained under the sovereignty of that crown, and was not brought back under the domain of its old Master until the beginning of the 18th century. This conquest and subjugation to the King of France was formerly not disadvantageous to it; for, when the Reformation began in France and was established, the King granted this Valley the same Freedom of Conscience <term>Freedom of Conscience: The right to follow one's religious beliefs without state interference.</term> that he allowed to the other Reformed subjects of his Realm, whereby it went very well for the Waldensians here.

This Valley then consisted of 8 congregations which, along with the others of the Alpine Mountains toward the side of Dauphiné <note>A former province in southeastern France.</note>, belonged under the Churches of Dauphiné, and together they made up one of the Provincial Synods of France. Because of this, these congregations were shielded against the persecutions that so violently devastated the three other Valleys in the 16th and 17th centuries. They

...rejoiced during those sorrowful times to be under France’s dominion, little thinking that this obedience to that Crown would afterwards make them doubly miserable.

They certainly underwent, like all Reformed Churches, a grievous and sad persecution after the revocation of the **Edict of Nantes** <note>The Edict of Nantes (1598) had granted French Protestants (Huguenots) substantial rights; its revocation in 1685 by Louis XIV led to intense persecution and mass emigration.</note> in the year 1685. Their churches were razed, the ministers were forced to flee, and they themselves were compelled to leave their fatherland and scatter everywhere. However, because at that time the rage against the Reformed was not as strong in this Valley as it was in other parts of that Kingdom, a multitude of them returned to their Valley after they had hidden themselves during the first storm-blast. They remained there until the year 1730, at which time more Reformed were counted there than Roman Catholics.

*Victor Amadeus* <note>Victor Amadeus II (1666–1732), Duke of Savoy and later King of Sicily and Sardinia.</note>, warring against France in the year 1708 and mastering the Valley of *Pragelas* at that time, renewed his old right that he had over it and held it in possession for himself, having no intention of ever giving it back. The *British* Court and **Their High Mightinesses** <note>original: "Hunne Hoog Mogende" — the formal title for the States General, the Dutch government.</note>, hearing of the capture of this Valley, immediately did their utmost to also provide the *Waldensians* living here with the same privileges that their brethren in the other Valleys enjoyed.

Queen *Anne* <note>Anne (1665–1714), Queen of Great Britain.</note> wrote to the Duke regarding this, and his answer was highly favorable; but he showed at the same time that it appeared more convenient to him, for several reasons, to postpone this step—which was so significant for him—until the conclusion of a Peace. From that time on, the *Waldensians* of *Pragelas* began to enjoy various advantages following that beneficial state of the times. <header>CHURCH HISTORY</header>

## XX. CHAPTER.

->*A detailed description of the contemporary state of the thirteen congregations in the Valleys, with which this Church History concludes.*<-

Thus I believe I have fulfilled my purpose in writing a SHORT CHURCH HISTORY OF THE WALDENSIANS UP TO THE PRESENT TIME. We have briefly traversed the earliest fortunes <note>The "earliest fortunes" refers to the medieval origins of the Waldensians and their survival through centuries of persecution prior to the Reformation.</note> and directed the reader to where he may find them recorded more extensively, as we had no desire to transcribe and reprint events of the early times that have already been described in our own language.

The significant events from the year 1686 <note>The year 1686 was a turning point, marking the brutal expulsion of the Waldensians from their valleys by Victor Amadeus II, followed by their "Glorious Return" in 1689.</note> up to the present time, we have presented more extensively in their principal circumstances, because the reader will find these nowhere else in our language. We have only omitted some details of little or no weight, seeing no necessity to create a great fuss and to describe in a thick and tedious folio <term>folio: a very large, heavy book made from full-sized sheets of paper, often associated with dense academic or legal texts</term> what could be shown in a short space, though perhaps with more effort.

In this, we followed somewhat in the footsteps of the Archbishop of Canterbury, who in the year 1761 was asked by the King of England <note>King George III.</note> about the present state of the *Waldensians*, whereupon that eminent man, in a short sketch of a few written pages, presented to his King all that had happened to that people from the year 1686 until that time. And although I have been more detailed in my narrative than that learned man—and in my judgment, rightly so, as I was not addressing a Monarch involved in weighty affairs of State

### First cause of their poverty.

As subjects, they are required to pay the charges known as the *Royal Impost* <term>Impost: a tax or duty imposed by a sovereign; in this context, it refers to the direct taxes levied by the Duke of Savoy</term>. ### Second cause of their poverty.

The young men who devote themselves to studies, with the intention of eventually holding the office of the ministry in the Valleys, are almost all from the Valley of *Lucerna* <note>Now known as the Val Pellice, the most central and accessible of the Waldensian valleys.</note>; thus, when they are called to the Valley of *St. Martin* <note>Now the Val Germanasca, which was more rugged and isolated.</note>, they soon try to move back to *Lucerna* as soon as a vacancy opens up, in order to have a more pleasant residence.

5. It becomes even more unpleasant for the ministers of the Valley of *St. Martin* when one of them dies. During the winter season, the survivor cannot receive any assistance from the ministers of *Lucerna* and *Perouse* <note>The Val Chisone.</note> to take turns preaching in the vacant pulpit—an advantage that those in the latter two valleys always enjoy by assisting one another. Thus, the remaining minister or ministers—for there are three congregations in this Valley—must either exhaust themselves by preaching for their own and then also for the vacant congregation, or leave the pulpit empty.

6. Although it is true that King William III <note>The Dutch Stadtholder and King of England, who was a champion of the Protestant cause.</note> and the States of the Netherlands obtained permission from the then-Duke in the year 1694 for the Valleys to employ foreign ministers in times of necessity, it is no less certain that this permission has long since fallen into disuse. Furthermore, the Synod of the Valleys seems to raise difficulties regarding the manner in which this practice could be reinstated. Thus, all ministers [must be] Wal-

### *Use of the Scholarships, established for the service of young men in study.*

Should it occur to the reader here that they have heard mention above of the founding of several scholarships (*) <margin>Page 157.</margin>, to assist young people in their studies, and should they ask if these are no longer in existence? 1. Are not enough to meet all the expenses of the studies. The parents are often not in a position to provide the additional funds the children require, which holds many back from pursuing their studies.

### A Short Account of the foreign assistance provided from time to time for the preservation of these Communities, and of what is done annually and specifically now to that end.

In order not to repeat what we have already mentioned in the appropriate places throughout our Narrative—namely, what various *Protestant Princes of Europe*, especially *King William III* <note>William of Orange (1650–1702), who served as Stadtholder of the Netherlands and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland.</note>, along with his consort *Queen Mary*, of most glorious memory, and the *States General of the Netherlands* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, did in the previous century for the preservation of the *Waldensians*, particularly when they were exhausted by severe persecutions or after enduring fearsome judgments—we nevertheless consider ourselves obliged to say a word in conclusion about what is still being done today for their rescue from the poverty and other misery they suffer.

The *Protestant Princes of Germany* currently offer no support to the Communities of the Valleys. The *Swiss* do not abandon the Valleys at all, but maintain the established <term>Bursaries|Beurzen: Scholarships or endowments intended to fund the education of students, typically for the ministry.</term> mentioned above, and thus from time to time provide the Valleys with young <term>Ministers|Leeraaren: Literally 'teachers,' but used here to denote clergy or pastors.</term> who have begun and completed their literary studies at their expense. The present *King of England*, who shows such great zeal for the Christian Religion and the well-being of the foreign churches, nobly continues to [pay] the 260 pounds sterling from the fund established by the late *Queen Mary* in the previous century, annually...

In the year 1740, so informs us the Reverend Mr. *Chatelain*, who for thirty-one years has maintained an unbroken correspondence with the Ministers of the Valleys, and despite his advancing years still continues therein: in the year 1740, the Gentlemen *Commissioners* received new reports regarding the pressing needs of the Churches in the Valleys (*). The States General of the Netherlands, not having strayed from the ancient generosity of their forefathers, nobly offered a gift of 12,000 guilders. Two Dutch <term>Synods|A regional or national council of church leaders.</term> gave proof of their love for suffering churches, and particularly those of the Valleys <note>The Waldensian Valleys in the Piedmont region of Italy.</note>. Middelburg, where no collection for the *Waldensians* had been held in the years 1729 and 1730, now seemed intent on leading other cities in generosity in an exemplary manner.

On the 12th day of <term>December|Wintermaand: An old Dutch name for the month of December.</term> of the previous year, the Honorable and Worshipful Magistrate of that city designated a general *collection* to be held. To better achieve their pious objective, that zealous government ensured that the Ministers, on the preceding Sunday, urged the congregation toward generous gifts through the most emphatic admonitions. The outcome lived up to these preparations. After the collection, it was calculated that 10,917 guilders, 10 pennies, and 8 cents had been given through the goodwill of Middelburg for the maintenance of the Congregations of the Valleys (*).

He praises the modesty of their conduct, their zeal for the Doctrine, and other good qualities. The passion for the purity of the Doctrine remains so great that the common people would rise up against the Teachers, should these men attempt to present to them a different Doctrine than that which they had received from their orthodox <note>In this context, "orthodox" refers to the Reformed or Calvinist faith shared by the Waldensians and the Dutch.</note> Ancestors.

## N O T E.

This following Discourse on <term>Church Discipline<note>Original Dutch: "Kerkelyke Tugt." This refers to the system of moral oversight and behavioral standards maintained by the church community to ensure members lived according to their faith.</note></term> was submitted for examination to the great Swiss Reformer <term>Bucerus<note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a key Protestant reformer who sought to mediate between different factions of the Reformation.</note></term> by the Ministers of the <term>Waldensians<note>A medieval Christian movement that preceded the Reformation, known for its emphasis on poverty and adherence to the Bible.</note></term>, and was honored by him with a laudable testimony. <term>Melanchthon<note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a major German Reformer and close collaborator of Martin Luther.</note></term> also could not refrain from giving his consent to it in the year 1559. It is drawn from very old manuscripts of the Ministers of the Valleys; however, the time when it was composed cannot be precisely determined. When one observes its entire course and compares the main points with the practices of the early Christians in the matter of Church Discipline, as presented to us by the early <term>Church Fathers<note>Ancient Christian theologians and leaders whose writings are considered foundational to the faith.</note></term>, one easily sees that it bears a great resemblance to the simplicity and conscientiousness observed in the early days of Christianity; thus we may say that it carries in every way the hallmarks of a venerable antiquity. The <term>Walloon Synod<note>The administrative assembly of French-speaking Reformed churches in the Netherlands.</note></term>, held at <term>Naarden<note>A fortified town in the Netherlands where this ecclesiastical meeting took place in 1668.</note></term> in the year 1668, has given it a Synodical Approval. We have taken the liberty to shorten some extensive Articles, for example the 8th and 9th, without, however, damaging the substance of the text. It is of the following content:

### *Rules which the ancient Teachers of the Waldensians used to preserve the purity of Doctrine, and to prevent all misconduct in life within their Communities.*

->A R T I C L E I.<-

->*Concerning Discipline.*<-

The <term>Doctrine of Discipline<note>Original Dutch: "Tugtleer." This refers to the systematic instruction and enforcement of moral conduct and church order.</note></term> encompasses the entire <term>Moral Law<note>Original Dutch: "Zeedeleer." The study or system of ethics and behavior based on Christian teachings.</note></term>, just as Christ and the Apostles taught it: namely, how every believer shall live in their <term>calling<note>In this context, "calling" or "vocation" refers to a person's profession or station in life, viewed as a duty to God.</note></term> and walk in all righteousness. Holy Scripture provides abundant instruction in this discipline to all people—no matter their status or age—and demonstrates at the same time that it is the bond of love and the means of agreement in practicing the <term>communion of Saints<note>The spiritual union and fellowship of all members of the Christian Church.</note></term>. Whoever wishes to have knowledge of these matters, let them read what the Apostles say regarding this in their epistles, and they shall receive extensive instruction on how everyone is obliged to preserve the bond of peace, and to walk in such a way that they give no offense, and do not cause their neighbor to fall, whether through wicked words or through evil crimes. They will find how everyone is obliged not only to flee from evil, but also to avoid the opportunity for evil; and if someone should have stumbled, how they may be set right and led toward <term>repentance<note>Original Dutch: "bekeering." Turning away from sin and toward God; a central theme in Waldensian life.</note></term>.

## ARTICLE II.

->Concerning the <term>Teachers<note>Original Dutch: "Leeraaren." In the Waldensian context, this refers to their ministers or pastors, who were primarily seen as teachers of the Word.</note></term>.<-

Whosoever wishes to be promoted to the <term>office of preaching<note>Original Dutch: "Predikampt." The specific vocation or formal role of a public preacher.</note></term> among us shall, while he is still young, as a proof of his humility, request of us to be accepted for it, and ask that we pray to God for him, so that he may receive the necessary ability for this weighty ministry.

To this end, we shall give him instruction and require him to learn by heart the Gospels of *Matthew* and *John*, as well as all the Epistles of the *Apostles*, and a large portion of the *Books of Solomon*, the *Psalms of David*, and the *Prophets*.

And when he is of good testimony, we shall, through the laying on of hands, grant him the freedom to perform public preaching services.

He who was most recently accepted into the ministry shall do nothing pertaining to his office without the knowledge of the one who was accepted before him; and likewise, the first, and so on with the others, may do nothing without the knowledge of his fellow brother <note>This suggests a system of mutual accountability and seniority, ensuring that no minister acted independently or without consultation.</note>; so that all matters among us may occur in good order.

Livelihood shall be given to him and to us voluntarily, yet sufficiently, by the good <term>congregation<note>Original Dutch: "Gemeinte." Referring to the local body of believers.</note></term> which we instruct.

Concerning the power which God has given to his servants, we establish that he has granted them the authority to appoint <term>fellow brothers<note>Original Dutch: "Medebroederen." Here referring to colleagues or elders in the church hierarchy.</note></term>, who govern the congregation, into the ministry, as the variety of occurring matters and unity in *Christ* require; just as *Paul* teaches *Titus 1: 5*. <note>The text provides a Dutch translation of the Latin Vulgate or a similar early version.</note> *For this cause I left you in Crete, that you might [set in order] what was still lacking*, and so forth.

## ARTICLE III.

->*Concerning the Education of Children.*<-

Children, who are born of sinful parents, must be born again of God through the means of discipline and instruction; wherefore *Solomon* admonishes: *withhold not correction from the child, for if you strike him with the rod, he shall not die; you shall strike him with the rod, and deliver his soul from hell.* <note>Original Dutch: "Tugt" (discipline/correction). The author is quoting Proverbs 23:13-14 to emphasize the necessity of moral instruction.</note> He who instructs his son shall be praised in him, and shall be glorified in the midst of his household. He who instructs his son makes his enemy jealous and is honored in the midst of his friends. If the father is deceased, he is as if he has not died, for he leaves behind one who is his likeness. <note>This section draws heavily from the wisdom of the book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 30:2-6, emphasizing the continuity of the family name through a well-raised heir.</note> As long as the father lives, he rejoices in his son during his lifetime, for he is neither shamed nor embarrassed, and in dying he is not grieved before the face of his enemies, for he has left behind protectors of the family against his enemies, and children who show gratitude to his friends.

Instruct your son in the fear of the Lord, in the ways of his statutes and laws.

Do not despair of your child when he is unwilling to receive your reproof and is not ready to improve himself: for your labor does not gather fruits from the field as soon as it is sown, but it awaits the proper time.

Once more: correct your children and guard your daughters—if you have them, guard their honor; for *Dinah*, *Jacob’s* daughter, lost

## ARTICLE IV.

### *Regarding Church Assemblies.*

We choose from the Congregation those who must rule: <term>Elders<note>Original Dutch: "Ouderlingen." In the Waldensian tradition, these were lay leaders chosen for their wisdom and character to oversee the spiritual and practical life of the community.</note></term>, according to the variety of occurring matters and the unity in *Christ* that such requires.
The money provided to us by the Congregation we bring into the great General Assembly (*), and we hand it over in the presence of all. When the Leaders of the Assembly have received it, there is, as much as is deemed good, distributed to the <term>Teachers<note>Original Dutch: "Leeraaren." These were the ordained ministers or missionary preachers of the Waldensians.</note></term> who are to undertake travels (†), and the other part is given to the poor.

### ARTICLE VII.

#### *Regarding Marriage.*

Marriage must be contracted outside the degrees of kinship, as God has instituted it, and not according to those which He has forbidden. <note>This refers to the biblical laws of consanguinity found in Leviticus. ## ARTICLE VII.

### Concerning Marriage.

Marriage must be contracted outside the <term>degrees of kinship<note>Historically, the church forbade marriage between close relatives. This text argues for following biblical rules rather than the more complex and often expensive rules set by the medieval Church.</note></term>, just as God has ordained, and not according to those whom He has forbidden. One should not make any difficulty regarding the regulations established by the *Pope* in this regard, much less worry that one has given him no money to obtain an exemption from the aforementioned regulations; for what God has not forbidden can take place without the *Pope*.

The solemnization of marriage ought not to take place without the consent of the parents on both sides, for the children are the property of their fathers and mothers.

## ARTICLE VIII.

### *Concerning the Taverns (*):*

A tavern is a source of all kinds of sins, a school of the Devil, where he performs his miracles. God shows His virtues in His Church, and proves His miracles there—namely, by enlightening the blind, making the lame walk, making the mute speak, and giving hearing to the deaf—but the Devil does the opposite in the taverns. If an excessive man or a <term>glutton<note>Dutch: *slemper*. A person who indulges in riotous eating and drinking; a carouser.</note></term> enters, he walks straight in his gait, but returning, he goes staggering, and has lost his sight, hearing, and speech. These are the miracles that the Devil performs in the taverns: the lessons given there are excess, drunkenness, perjury, lies, slander, the denial of God, and other sins. Taverns stir up quarrels, disagreements, and homicides; and the <term>innkeepers<note>Dutch: *Waarden*. The hosts or proprietors of public houses.</note></term> who maintain such houses share in the sins committed there.

HEADER: CHURCH HISTORY.

...the old Teachers of the *Waldensians* <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement that sought to return to the simplicity of the early church, often facing persecution for their beliefs.</note> rail vehemently against dancing. One can see most clearly how very committed they were to the ancient dignity and modesty of Christians. They demonstrate that the dances, at that time very much in vogue among the *Roman Catholics*, were contrary to all the Commandments of the two Tables of the Law of God. These dance styles were likely brought over from voluptuous *Italy* into the Valleys <note>Referring to the Alpine valleys of Piedmont where the Waldensian communities were primarily located.</note>, and were much practiced on the Lord’s day. After they have strongly loathed these and earnestly warned their congregations against them, they close this Article with *Augustine’s* words:
> *Wretched one, do you not know that for as many steps as you take in the dance, you also approach hell by as many strides.* <note>original: "elendige, weet gy niet, dat zo veele treden gy in den dans maakt, gy ook met zo veele schreeden tot de hel nadert." This quote is traditionally attributed to St. Augustine in medieval moral treatises to discourage revelry.</note>

### A R T I C L E X.

#### *How the Congregation must behave in daily interaction with those who are outside.*

1. One must not love the World.
2. Bad company must be avoided.
3. As much as is possible, keep peace with all men.
4. Avoid matters of dispute.
5. One must not avenge oneself.
6. Love one’s enemies.
7. Out of love for the truth, one must be willing to endure all difficulties, slanders, threats, banishment, reproach, mistreatment, and all kinds of torment.
8. One must possess one’s soul in patience.
9. Do not take up the yoke with unbelievers. <note>A reference to the biblical instruction in 2 Corinthians 6:14 to not be "unequally yoked" with those who do not share the faith.</note>
10. Have no fellowship with the works of darkness, and especially not with those which have any semblance of <term>Idolatry<note>The worship of idols or excessive devotion to something other than God; here, it likely refers to Roman Catholic rituals which the Waldensians viewed as superstitious.</note></term>, or give occasion for it.

### ARTICLE VIII.
### *Concerning Drinking Houses (*).*

A drinking house is a source of all kinds of sins, a school of the Devil, where he performs his wonders. God displays His virtues in His Church and demonstrates His wonders there—namely, in enlightening the blind, making the lame walk, making the mute speak, and giving hearing to the deaf; but the Devil does the opposite in the drinking houses. Drinking houses provoke quarrels, discord, and murders; and the innkeepers <note>original: "Waarden"</note> who maintain such houses share in the sins committed therein.

# CHURCH HISTORY.

the ancient teachers of the *Waldensians* rail violently against dancing. One can see most clearly how much they were set upon the old dignity and modesty of Christians. They demonstrate that dances—which were very much in fashion among the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Roomschen"</note> at that time—were contrary to all the Commandments of the two Tables of the Law of God. These dance styles were likely brought into the Valleys from lustful *Italy* and were often practiced on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>. > *Wretch, do you not know that for every step you take in the dance, you also approach hell by as many strides?* <note>original: "elendige, weet gy niet, dat zo veele treden gy in den dans maakt, gy ook met zo veele schreeden tot de hel nadert." This is a Dutch translation of a sentiment often attributed to St. Augustine in medieval moral treatises.</note>

## ARTICLE XI.

### *How* Believers *shall govern themselves.*

1. They must not satisfy the lusts of the flesh.
2. They must take care that their members <note>Refers to the parts of the body, as in the biblical "instruments of righteousness" from Romans 6:13.</note> are weapons of righteousness.
3. Govern their judgment and senses well.
4. Subject the body to the Spirit.
5. Mortify <note>original: "dooden" - literally "to kill," a theological term for suppressing sinful nature.</note> their members.
6. Avoid idleness.
7. Love temperance in food, drink, and in the care for worldly matters, and be prudent in words.
8. Not forget works of mercy.
9. Live in all holiness through Faith.
10. Fight against lusts and sensuality.
11. Mortify the works of the flesh.
12. Redeem <note>original: "uitkoopen" - literally "to buy out," echoing the biblical phrase to "redeem the time."</note> proper time for religious exercises.
13. Consult with one another regarding the will of God.
14. Diligently examine one’s conscience.
15. Purify, improve, and pacify one’s Spirit.

...is allowed as a Father or Witness <note>In this context, "Witness" refers to a godparent or sponsor at a baptism.</note> to offer his Child for baptism. No Marriage is solemnized for Persons who are not Members of the Church. Those who make themselves guilty of grave crimes are not received into the bosom of the Church until they have given clear evidence of their improvement.

For three consecutive Sundays, such Church members are placed in a special seat <note>original: "byzondere geſtoelte" — likely a "penitent’s stool" or a specific bench located prominently in front of the congregation.</note> before the Pulpit in view of the entire Congregation: after the Sermon, before the Teacher <term>Leeraar: in this context, the Minister or Pastor</term> blesses the People, he informs his Congregation that such a Person has committed such a crime, and is making a public confession thereof—this being done, the penitent throws himself upon his knees and, on the first Sunday, listens in that posture to what the Teacher brings to his attention regarding the shamefulness of his crime and the judgment of God, of which he has made himself worthy—on the second Sunday, the Teacher shows the penitent the necessity of true conversion and its salutary consequences—on the third Sunday, the penitent prays with a loud voice to God and the Congregation for forgiveness of the committed crime, and promises henceforth to provide more edification <note>original: "ſtigting" — meaning moral or spiritual improvement and being a good example to others.</note> to the Congregation than the offense he previously caused—whereupon the Teacher announces to him, in the name of God, the forgiveness of Sins and reunification with the Church,

---

and after having given a hearty exhortation to holiness to the Congregation—so that he who stands might take heed that he does not fall—the Teacher ends with Prayer.

In case of fornication <note>original: "hoerery" — a broad term used in historical church law to cover various acts of sexual immorality, including adultery or pre-marital relations.</note>, the same Ecclesiastical ceremony is observed, yet only for two Sundays.

### APPENDICES TO THE

When someone, out of weakness or other reasons, has abandoned the Religion <note>Referring here to the Waldensian or Reformed faith.</note> and attended Mass; he is not accepted back into the Congregation unless he has, in the same manner, made confession of Sins and penance: — but anyone who has left the *Romish* <note>original: "Roomsche" — a common historical term for the Roman Catholic Church.</note> Doctrine and embraces the pure Doctrine is obliged to make the abjuration <note>A formal renunciation of former beliefs under oath.</note> before the full Congregation.

The same Ecclesiastical discipline is observed regarding those who profane the Lord’s day.

All games of *Chance* are forbidden, and whoever sins against this prohibition must do penance according to the circumstances of the transgression.

All Dances <note>original: "Dansreyen" — specifically referring to group or round dances.</note> are forbidden and are not forgiven without performing public penance: to the latter are also held those who have watched the dancing of the *Roman Catholics* from afar, without having taken part in it themselves.

*Leger* <note>Jean Léger (1615–1670), a prominent pastor and historian known for his work on the history of the Waldensian churches.</note> says he knew one of the most prominent Teachers <term>Leeraaren: Ministers or Pastors</term> of the Valleys, whose Wife—without intending any harm—had allowed herself to be led by a *French* Lady (who was one of her relatives) while walking, to the place where the *Romanists* were busy dancing. She had viewed their merriment from afar, whereupon her husband found himself obliged, according to the Ecclesiastical Law, to summon one of the neighboring Teachers to preside over a specially convened Consistory Meeting <term>Kerkenraads Vergaadering: a governing body of a local church consisting of the minister and elders</term>, and to bring his own Wife under censure <note>In this context, a formal ecclesiastical "reprimand" or disciplinary action.</note>.

I can, says *Leger*, by the grace of God say—without flattering my Fatherland (namely the Valleys), as those who know it can judge for themselves—that there are no *Reformed* Churches where the word of God is heard with more zeal, humility, and diligence;

---

(*) This last digit was so worn in the *Act* <note>The formal commission document.</note> of King *William* that one had to guess what was written there. I first thought that it had been given to *Arnaud* in the year 1690. *William* did, after all, cross over from *England* to *Holland* at the beginning of that year; as is especially well known from the mortal danger that Prince faced on the *Dutch* coast. For when he arrived in the *Meuse* <note>The Maas river</note> and it was judged that two hours of rowing could bring him to land, he, being weary of the sea, sat in an open boat; but due to mist and storm, he wandered for over sixteen hours before he reached land safely. However, it soon became clear to me that this *Act* was not given at the time of the King's crossing when I recalculated the years of his reign, which was then not the third, but the first. I then concluded that the *Act* was issued in the month of *March* of the year 1692 by King *William*, while he was in The Hague, in which I was strengthened by *Burnet’s* <note>Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury and a close advisor to William III, known for his historical writings.</note> account, which informs us that the King crossed from *England* to *Holland* in that month to make preparations for an early campaign. I did not want to overlook this trifle, because it shows that King *William* did not elevate *Arnaud* to that significant post until after he had seen more clearly from his campaigns with the Duke of *Savoy* how much that Pastor <note>Henri Arnaud remained a minister of the church even while leading troops.</note> was worthy of such a promotion.

(*) This last digit was so worn away in the *Act* <term>Act: a formal decree or commission</term> of King *William* that one had to guess what was written there. I first thought that it had been given to *Arnaud* in the year 1690. *William* did indeed cross over from *England* to *Holland* at the beginning of that year; as is particularly well-known from the mortal danger that the Prince faced on the *Dutch* coast. For when he arrived at the *Meuse* <note>The Maas river</note>, and it was judged that two hours of rowing could bring him to land, he—being weary of the sea—sat in an open boat; but through fog and storm he wandered for over sixteen hours before he arrived safely on land. However, it soon became clear to me that this *Act* was not given at the time of the King's crossing when I recalculated the years of his reign, which at that time was not the third, but the first. I then concluded that the *Act* was issued in the month of *March* of the year 1692 by King *William*, being then in The Hague. In this I was strengthened by *Burnet's* <note>Bishop Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), a close advisor to William and author of "History of His Own Time."</note> account, which informs us that the King crossed from *England* to *Holland* in that month to make preparations for an early campaign. I did not want to overlook this small detail, because it shows that King *William* did not elevate *Arnaud* to that significant post until after he had seen more clearly from his campaigns with the Duke of *Savoy* <note>The Waldensians fought alongside the Duke of Savoy's forces against the French after the Duke joined the Grand Alliance.</note> how much that Minister <note>Arnaud was a pastor-colonel; the term "Leeraar" refers to his clerical status.</note> was worthy of such a promotion.

to defend against the accusations of the famous **BOSSUET** <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704) was a powerful French Catholic bishop and theologian who famously attacked Protestant history, arguing the Waldensians were late-arriving heretics rather than a continuous line of "true" Christians.</note>. And no one, as far as I know, has undertaken in this 18th century to write a continuation of those histories, although enough material has remained.

ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF THE WALDENSIANS. 11

### REMARK. (*)

On page 21, line 1 from the top, after the word: *Century*.

I must acknowledge that the fortunes of the Waldensians in the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, and the first half of the 17th Century, which I have treated briefly, highly deserve a more detailed description. To my knowledge, a continuous history of them does not exist in any other language. Upon the first edition of my work, I did intend to take this great period of history more closely into hand in the future. However, it has been impossible for me thus far. Seeing once again that all historians have left me in want of information here, I requested the current ministers of the Valleys <note>The Alpine valleys of Piedmont, the traditional home of the Waldensians.</note> to offer me the necessary assistance; but they too, they say, lack the authentic documents, because all the old records relating to this period were scattered or burned by enemies during the subsequent severe persecutions. It is therefore to be feared that an opportunity will never arise to perform this remarkable service for the Church.

---

On page 21, line 3 from the top, after the word: *out*.

They spread throughout *Italy* in the year 1229. Under the jurisdiction of *Venice*, they had established seven schools, which were supported by their fellow believers from *Lombardy*, who perhaps thereby brought the Pope's hatred upon themselves. At the very least, at the insistence of his Legate <note>A papal legate is a personal representative of the Pope, often sent with high authority to handle specific ecclesiastical or political matters.</note>, they had to be banished from the cities and villages there in that year, and their houses razed to the ground (*). Emperor **FREDERICK** <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor, who frequently clashed with the papacy despite his own edicts against heresy.</note> must also have complained about them to Pope **GREGORY** <note>Pope Gregory IX (reigned 1227–1241), known for institutionalizing the Inquisition.</note> in the year 1235, as a persecution in *Italy* followed.

The expansion of the *Waldensians* <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement that advocated for poverty and a return to the teachings of the early Church; they were frequently targeted by the Catholic Church as heretics.</note> in the *14th* Century is astonishing. ## ADDITION.

*On page 27, line 9 from the top, after the word: suffering.*

Among others, FRANCISCUS VARAGLIA, formerly a Capuchin <note>A reform branch of the Franciscan order, known for their brown robes and austerity.</note>, famous among the Roman Catholics for his persecuting spirit—which he seemed to have inherited from his father, who gave many proofs of it in the year 1488—had to suffer martyrdom. This man, while first attacking the doctrine of the *Waldensians* <note>A medieval Christian movement that sought a return to Apostolic simplicity; they were declared heretical by the Catholic Church and suffered centuries of persecution.</note> with the strongest arguments, found himself forced, upon considering their proofs, to pay homage to the truth and cross over to them. From then on he became one of their ministers, laboring as zealously to strengthen them in the faith as he had previously sought to tear it down, until he, seized with several other *Waldensians*, was thrown into prison in Turin, and finally condemned to the fire. GERDES <note>Daniel Gerdes (1698–1765), a Dutch theologian and historian of the Reformation.</note> gives us not only the comforting letter written by CALVIN <note>John Calvin, the influential French reformer in Geneva.</note> to the shackled man in prison, but also the confession he gave to his enemies during interrogation, and the discourse he delivered in the flames to the spectators of his martyrdom, which occurred in the year 1558: all are worthy of reading (*). The man’s death was a mournful event for the Valleys <note>The Piedmontese Alpine valleys, the ancestral home of the Waldensian community.</note>, due to the loss of the services received from him. Nor was that all; they lost two more of their countrymen shortly thereafter, in the year 1560: JOHANNES ALOYSIUS PASCHALIS <note>Also known as Giovan Luigi Paschale, a former soldier turned Waldensian pastor.</note>, who was burned at Rome, and JACOBUS BONELLUS <note>Giacomo Bonello, a Waldensian preacher from Calabria.</note>, who was burned at Messina. They were both ministers, preaching the word in Italy. (†)

### LETTER FROM THE STATES GENERAL OF THE NETHER-LANDS TO THE DUKE OF SAVOY, &c. <note>The States General was the sovereign governing body of the Dutch Republic, representing the seven united provinces.</note>

## MOST SERENE DUKE!

The Letter which it has pleased Your Royal Highness to write to us on the 19th of the Grass Month <note>April</note> of this year, having only been delivered to us in the Wine Month <note>October</note>, we have not been able to reply to it earlier, nor express our gratitude for the effort which Your Highness has been willing to take, to converse with us regarding your feelings concerning the state of affairs in the Valley of *Lucerna* <note>One of the primary Waldensian valleys in Piedmont.</note>, with respect to those who profess the same Religion as ourselves. We are sufficiently convinced of the goodness and justice of Your Royal Highness, to believe that you would wish to use force against neither the one nor the other, nor to oppress the innocent, nor to persecute Religion contrary to the word given to your Subjects. Neither is it our aim to speak for criminals and rebels; and one shall never be able to accuse us of having favored mutiny under the pretext of coming to the aid of the miserable: but, just as we take into consideration that there is no Judge who cannot be misled by the malice of the parties, so we also know that it is impossible for a Prince, however enlightened he may be, to discover all the deceits which men use against their enemies. Your Royal Highness knows that those who have set themselves up as accusers against your Subjects of the Valleys of *Piedmont* are no less their Enemies than those who...

At this time *HEIDEGGER* <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss theologian and influential figure in the Reformed Church.</note> assured *JURIEU* <note>Pierre Jurieu, a leader of the Huguenot exiles in the Netherlands.</note>—who had emphatically recommended the surviving *Waldenses* <note>A Protestant group from the Alpine valleys who faced severe persecution and displacement.</note> to him—in a letter dated the 6th of <term>July <note>original: "Hooimaand," the traditional Dutch name for the hay-harvest month.</note></term> of the year 1687, that they were very close to his heart. He stated that he and many others were devoting all their care to ensure they were not scattered, which would cause them to cease to exist as a community. *JURIEU* had feared this very thing. However, due to the treaty made between the Duke <note>Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy.</note> and the *Swiss*, and because of the dense population of the Swiss lands, he further explained that these people could not remain in *Switzerland*. The Cantons therefore thought it best to let them depart for *Württemberg*, which was situated nearby, and where they could be provided for and protected. Its Duke, *FREDERICK CHARLES* <note>Frederick Charles, Duke of Württemberg-Winnental, who served as regent.</note>, was uncommonly well-disposed toward them and had already summoned their leaders to visit and inspect the districts where he intended to settle them. *HEIDEGGER* says further that fifty of the leading *Waldenses*, accompanied by a Swiss envoy, were now ready to travel there, and he hoped for a desirable outcome.

### A TESTIMONIAL GIVEN BY THE PASTORS OF THE VALLEYS TO MR. ARNAUD AND HIS FAMILY UPON THEIR DEPARTURE FROM THERE.

We, Ministers of the <term>Waldenses <note>A proto-Protestant Christian movement that originated in the 12th century; they faced severe persecution and eventually joined the Reformation.</note></term>, Elders of the Evangelical Church at *St. Jean* <note>Modern-day San Giovanni Pellice in Italy.</note>, and Governors of the Valleys of *Piedmont*, declare and testify that Mr. **HENRY ARNAUD**, son of the late Mr. **FRANCIS ARNAUD**, hailing from the city of *Embrun* in *Dauphiné*, is originally a *Piedmontese*, as he is the son of the late Madam **MARGARET GROS**, born of an illustrious and noble lineage which formerly resided at *Dronero* in the *Marquisate* of *Saluzzo*. —Who in his early youth was raised in the schools of these Valleys to learn the first <term>liberal arts <note>original: "beschaafde Weetenschappen"; referring to the classical humanities curriculum of the time.</note></term>: subsequently, he was sent to the University of *Basel* to continue his literary studies there, enjoying the benevolent support which the illustrious rulers of that Canton were pleased to grant to our students: from there he traveled to *Holland*, and returned to the University of *Geneva* to complete his literary studies there. After this, he was accepted as a Minister by our Synod in the year 1670, along with Mr. **WILLIAM MALANOT**. The ministry of the Church at *Maneille* and *Macel* <note>Villages in the Germanasca Valley, part of the Waldensian territories.</note> was subsequently entrusted to him in the first instance, and thereafter those of several others of the principal congregations in our three Valleys; the latter being where he is currently a Minister, and which he is obliged to leave, to our great sorrow, in obedience to the commands...

[be informed] how, through the intrusion of Popish <note>original: 'Paapsche'. This was a derogatory term used by Protestants at the time for Roman Catholics, reflecting the era's sharp sectarian divisions.</note> Priests, the practice of their religion is being made difficult; that even in the Valley of Perosa <note>original: 'Perouse'</note> and Pragelato <note>original: 'Pragelas'</note>, no ministers of the holy Gospel are tolerated any longer; and that there is a desire to demand and force upon them the religion of their Sovereign <note>Referring to the Duke of Savoy, who was Catholic.</note>, despite their ancient liberty and recently obtained restoration. Therefore, we have recalled to mind how Your High Mightinesses <note>The formal title for the States General, the governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, according to your godly zeal for the glory of God and the expansion of the holy Gospel, are so heartily mindful of the suffering confessors of our most holy Faith, for their redemption and comfort. Consequently, we, according to the bounden duty of love toward our aforementioned fellow believers in the Piedmontese Valleys, cannot refrain from very earnestly requesting Your High Mightinesses—as is done herewith—that you may be pleased to employ your good offices with His Royal Highness, the Lord Duke of Savoy, whether during the upcoming peace negotiations (according to reports) or, should those not proceed, by other means, so that the aforementioned good people are not only not harmed in their ancient freedom of religion, but are also restored to the free exercise thereof. Your High Mightinesses' great influence with His Royal Highness leaves us with no doubt regarding a happy outcome; and the great God is unfailingly a rewarder of this shown grace. And we pray to His Divine Omnipotence that He may preserve Your High Mightinesses in ever-flourishing prosperity and blessing.

Written on the 1st of December <note>original: 'Wintermaand', an old Dutch name for December.</note> 1711.

Meanwhile, this Valley remained in distressing circumstances, until the late Mr. VAN HOEY, Dutch <note>original: "Hollandsche"</note> Ambassador to the Court of *France*, received a Memorandum regarding the oppressed Churches in the Valleys of *Pragelas*, *Zezane*, and *Chateau-daufin* from the Minister DU MONT. In this document, it was brought to his attention that these Valleys had been taken from *France* in the year 1708 by the armies of the Duke of *Savoy*, united with those of the Emperor, *England*, *Prussia*, and the States General <note>The "States General" (Staten-Generaal) was the governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>. VAN DER MEER and CHETWIN, the Dutch and English Envoys, who had subsequently assured them that the Duke had bound himself by a Treaty to grant freedom of religion to all lands he should conquer, and that they were free to hold their religious services in public, just as they had done under *France's* rule before the revocation of the Edict of *Nantes* <note>The Edict of Nantes (1598) granted French Protestants rights, but its revocation in 1685 by Louis XIV led to intense persecution.</note>.

Amst. 1731.* In this one finds, after a brief Description of that famous People, a List of the Texts, preached on the 9th of September <note>original: "Herfstmaand" — an old Dutch name for September, 'harvest month.'</note> of the year 1731 by all the Ministers of *Amsterdam*, in preparation for and recommendation of this Collection; — a list of the names of the Elders and Deacons who, by order of the Burgomasters, performed this Collection the following day; — with the names of twenty-five districts, where and how much each collected therein. The gathered Pennies in the City amounted to a sum of one hundred and thirty-one thousand, two hundred, and thirty-seven guilders, and four stuivers <note>A significant sum in the 18th century, equivalent to millions of dollars today.</note>: outside the City, an additional one thousand three hundred seventy-seven guilders and sixteen stuivers were collected from the Outskirts <note>original: "Cingels" — the residential areas just outside the city walls.</note> by the Officers of the Companies. At this time, the Collection also took place in the other *Hollandic Cities.*

The *Deputies of Holland* <note>Representatives of the Province of Holland within the States General.</note> undertook to bring this proposal into their State Assembly and deliberate upon it. And, when the *Swiss* renewed that request once more, the *States General* resolved to write to them (*): that from the beginning, great difficulties had arisen, and still arose, against receiving, placing, and providing maintenance for the fugitive Valley-dwellers <note>original: "Dallieden" — referring to the inhabitants of the Waldensian valleys in the Alps.</note>, if they all came over together; but that those who had the inclination and ability to settle in these lands were free to come over hither, and that those who needed some assistance would be provided for according to the circumstances. ### *Third cause of the decline of these Churches.*

KEISZLER (*) <note>Johann Georg Keyssler (1693–1743) was a German scholar and travel writer famous for his detailed accounts of European culture and geography.</note> provides yet another specific cause which may give much occasion for the apostasy of the Poor <note>A reference to the Waldensians, historically known as the "Poor of Lyon."</note>. Namely, there has been established in *Turin* a *Maison des Vaudois dans la Place Coraline* <note>French: "House of the Waldensians in the Piazza Carlina." This was the *Ospizio dei Catecumeni*, an institution designed to convert non-Catholics through social pressure and education.</note>, which is to say, a house of God for the impoverished *Waldenses*. In this house, they—especially children who present themselves voluntarily to convert to the Roman Faith—are received, instructed, and maintained, so that they should not need to beg. Efforts are made to marry off the girls when they grow up, and the boys are taught trades by which they can later earn their bread.

— Since the year 1765, that is, after the publication of the first edition of this History, the condition of these Churches throughout all Provinces and Synods of our Fatherland <note>The Dutch Republic (the United Provinces).</note> has been taken to heart in the most laudable manner, and this continues to this day. ...Waldenses in the old orthodox Doctrine. Regarding this, we have previously, for the sake of brevity, only appealed to a Letter—read by me—written by a prominent *Dutch* Gentleman living in one of our principal cities; who, on his journey to *Italy*, passing through the Valleys, investigated everything there, and afterwards reported on his experiences from *Rome* to one of his friends here: he spoke very extensively in praise of the simple, modest *Waldenses* who firmly adhere to the pure orthodox Doctrine. I have also added, in a word, what I knew from very authentic documents, namely, that the passion of those *Valley-dwellers* <note>Referring to the inhabitants of the Waldensian Valleys in the Piedmontese Alps.</note> for the purity of the doctrine remained so great that the Congregations would rise up against their Ministers if they dared to attempt to present them with a doctrine other than that which they received from their orthodox forefathers. 

Besides many other proofs, I wish now, for the sake of completeness, to further report that we have seen, and for a long time had in our possession, the *Principal Articles* of our Reformed Doctrine, signed by the thirteen Ministers of the Valleys with their own hands and confirmed with each of their seals. That document was afterwards handed over to the Noble and Mighty Gentleman who was deputed as *Political Commissioner* <note>A government official appointed by the civil authorities to attend church synods and ensure that ecclesiastical decisions did not conflict with state laws.</note> by the *States of Holland* <note>The governing body of the Province of Holland, the most influential province of the Dutch Republic.</note> to the *Synod of South Holland*; he, on that occasion, offered it to all who had a desire to read it, to be assured of its agreement with the confession of our Churches. And that document is still carefully preserved in good hands as a *Monument* of their pure Faith.

ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF THE WALDENSIANS.

# C O N C L U S I O N

Let us, rejoiced by the pleasant contemplation of this already much-improved state of those Churches, never fail to offer up our prayers to the great King of the Church, the ever-caring and watchful Lord, who has chosen the Valleys of Piedmont—low and contemptible places in the eyes of the world—to uphold the pure Gospel, preserved there in spite of all Enemies from the times of the Apostles until this day; let us, I say, offer our prayers to the mighty Lord of the Church, that He might so bless the current efforts, applied in unison by the Ministers <note>original: "Leeraaren"; referring to the clergy of the Dutch Reformed Church.</note> of our Fatherland and the English Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge <note>original: "Engelsche Maatschappy ter voortplanting van de kennisse des Christendoms"; refers to the SPCK, which provided significant financial and educational support to the Waldensians.</note>, that not only the destruction of those ancient, famous Congregations may be prevented forever, but also that the future prosperity of those Churches may draw its origin from it; that the supported Valley-dwellers <note>original: "Dallieden"; the inhabitants of the Waldensian valleys in the Cottian Alps.</note> may live holily and gratefully to the great Benefactor for these happy outcomes; and that it be granted to them to preserve the Doctrine of Truth, inviolate, until the world’s end, so that, to the shame of increasing, arrogant Unbelief, to the honor of the precious Gospel, and to the glory of the great Redeemer, **Jesus** **Christ**, they may have this boast: that from His first to His second and final coming, they have kept His word, and no one has taken their crown!

### ADDITION.

— A prominent Gentleman in The Hague <note>original: "'s Haage"; the seat of government in the Netherlands.</note> has, at my request, made every effort to obtain the Original Decree <note>original: "Acte"; a formal legal or administrative document.</note> signed by King **WILLIAM'S** <note>William III (1650–1702), Prince of Orange and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland, who was a key protector of the Protestant cause.</note> own hand, and to send me a transcript of it; however, after a long and fruitless search among the records preserved there—specifically those granted by that Prince to military officers—it occurred to him that the document must reside in the Chancery of England. This becomes quite clear when one considers the date. That Monarch issued the decree then, not in his capacity as the Stadtholder of the Netherlands <note>original: "Stadhouder"; the hereditary chief magistrate and military commander of the Dutch Republic.</note>, but as the King of England. Furthermore, the descendants of **ARNAUD** <note>Henri Arnaud (1641–1721), the pastor and military leader famous for leading the Waldensians back to their Piedmontese valleys during the "Glorious Return."</note> have also been unable to find the Decree he received from the King among the family papers still in their possession. For these reasons, I have compensated for this deficiency by providing the document shared above, which sufficiently fulfills the intended purpose.
